entries: Aspiring Mangaka is an M1 Merchant that focuses on winning interactions against the opponent by putting them in a disadvantageous position. He accomplishes this by using key tools in his kit. [i]Clairvoyance: Prediction[/i] is essential for forcing the opponent to waste their side dashes, limiting their approach options and making M1 trades more favorable for Aspiring Mangaka. On top of that, he also has [i]Oracle[/i], giving him access to Perfect Blocking and further improving his performance in M1 trades. After winning an M1 trade, Aspiring Mangaka can land [i]Shut Up![/i], which is an effective evasive-baiting tool. It forces the opponent to either use their evasive or take a large combo, as the move's evasive window is shorter than its stun duration, if the opponent does not evade early, they are unable to do so afterward, leaving them vulnerable. [i]Eye Catching[/i] is another defensive layer in Aspiring Mangaka's kit. Beyond the normal utility of a counter, [i]Eye Catching[/i] does not enter cooldown when successfully landed, making it a reliable option for defending against strong neutral tools from other characters and leveling the field. [i]Sacrilege[/i] is another useful tool that benefits from the opponent's limited side dash options. After forcing the opponent to waste their side dash, [i]Sacrilege[/i] can almost guarantee a hit against opponents without a counter. It provides consistent chip damage while also allowing for a combo conversion, as [i]Clairvoyance[/i] extends the ragdoll duration of [i]Sacrilege[/i], allowing Aspiring Mangaka to convert it into [i]Despair[/i] with a side dash.

Black Death is a big-body character that's able to control the neutral at most ranges, their tools aiding them in M1 trading, denying approaches, approaching themselves, and generally forcing the opponent to play their game. Unlike the rest of the cast, most of Black Death's damage comes in the form of their [b]Injury[/b] gimmick: a DoT effect that detonates into instant damage once its gauge is completely filled. Overall, Black Death has a powerful neutral game in exchange for backloaded damage.

Black Death's neutral is particularly strong thanks to all of their moves having some use inside it, be it in one way or another: - [b]Festering Strikes[/b] is a source of safe-on-block chip damage, aswell as a way to skip M1 trades by using its parrying property. - [b]Detach[/b] is a quick, safe poke with decent reward; it also can hit the opponent from behind if curved. - [b]Roach Swarm[/b] is an unblockable poke or gap closer depending on the variant, with damage that scales on [b]Injuries[/b]. - [b]Chokehold[/b] is a risky callout to opponents who try and disrespect your pressure (use VERY sparingly!!!). - [b]Earthen Insect Trance[/b] is mostly just a distraction tool, although it deals a tiny amount of chip damage. Depending on the situation, Black Death can go for a more aggresive, pressure-heavy gameplan by rushing the opponent with [b]Aerial Roach Swarm[/b] and pressuring them with [b]Festering Strikes[/b], or go for a more passive, poke-based one by checking their opponent's approach attempts with [b]Detach[/b] and regular [b]Roach Swarm[/b]. The playstyle they should adapt is often influenced by their opponent's character, but usually they'll get better results from alternating between both.

Black Death should land Detach on the opponent on basically any combo they do, unless it was previously on cooldown; that being said, there's always a chance for them to land it in neutral as a poke. Regardless of the way it lands on the opponent, it will give Black Death access to [b]Reattach[/b]. And when they use [b]Reattach[/b] on a ragdolled opponent, they drag the poor soul right onto their face, not only allowing Black Death themselves to always land an M1 before the opponent, but also wasting their wakeup invencibility during the pull, making being this close a much bigger threat than if they were to just be M1'd on a regular wakeup. This allows Black Death to bully and/or mix them up in many ways: OPTION BEATS... INFO M1 from the front Mashing on wakeup, blocking behind Shouldn't be used on the first Reattach oki, as most opponents will hold block on it. Use once the opponent is conditioned to block behind themselves or if they often try to fight back. M1 from behind Blocking front Very solid and reliable option. The opponent will often adapt to it, opening them up to M1s from the front and enabling 50/50s. Point blank [b]Roach Swarm[/b] All blocking Once the opponent gets used to blocking, Black Death may add [b]Roach Swarm[/b] into the mix to increase the opponent's mental stack. Should they worry about where they should block? Should they even block at all? [b]Festering Strikes[/b] Blocking (partially), mashing (partially) While it won't offer as much value as regular M1 hits, it's hard to ever go wrong with this option. [b]M1 + Chokehold[/b] M1 trading attempts If the opponent always retaliates with an M1 after successfully blocking Black Death's 50/50, they may leave themselves open to this option. If this lands, it might scare them into holding block for longer while pressured; allowing Black Death to go for two of any of the previous options in a row. If it DOESN'T land, they'll be heavily punished. It's a high-risk, high-reward option. Blocking (or dodging) Counters, reversals, mashing (partially) When fighting a character with a counter, such as Vessel or Aspiring Mangaka, or an invincible move, such as Head of the Hei or True Cannon, the best move can sometimes be to do nothing. Watch them waste their counter or reversal and open themselves up to a combo (or at least to more pressure). Of course, this will also protect the user from mashing, but it'll just be like a normal M1 trade after that. It's worth mentioning that Black Death won't always have all of these tools available (especially after... well, a full combo), but just the ability to 50/50 with M1s while having real priority makes [b]Reattach[/b] okizeme pretty powerful. The rest of their options just help it make a tad bit more scary to deal with.

Black Death do three slashes with slight forward momentum, the final slash launching the opponent on hit or block. Each slash will inflict its injury even through block, and can parry melee attacks. However, it has tremendous endlag on whiff.

Besides being Black Death's main combo filler, [b]Festering Strikes[/b] is a decent neutral tool at a close range, which stems from its dominance over other melee options (blocking included) and the fact that it applies full Injury stacks even on block. When blocked, it's launches the opponent away without stunning them, making it a good way to go back to neutral and prevent the opponent from taking their turn in an M1 trade. It [i]is[/i] possible for the opponent to dash away before the third hit and leave Black Death very vulnerable, so it's better to not abuse it against knowledgeable opponents. Another great property it has is the ability to parry M1s (one for each hit), allowing Black Death to quickly get out of block pressure, and potentially even get a cheeky hit against opponents who don't expect this option. It's overall a good close-range option for defense or block pressure, but it should only be used at very close range to make sure it doesn't whiff. Else, the resulting endlag could be [i]catastrophic[/i].

Once Black Death lands an M1, [b]Festering Strikes[/b] is their main Injury building combo tool, dealing many Injury stacks and a ragdoll that can combo into anything other than [b]Roach Swarm Explosion[/b]. However, its most interesting followup is [b]Chokehold[/b]. If [b]Chokehold[/b] is timed just right during the final slash, it can create a fully unevasiveable combo. A lot of players will attempt to evasive anyways to call out a failed timing... but the user may instead not use [b]Chokehold[/b] at all, making for a decent evasive bait.

If R is pressed during the startup of [b]Festering Strikes[/b], or if they're unarmed after using [b]Detach[/b], Black Death will instead throw two punches, followed by a slower, unblockable sweep; this causes the move to deal more damage and no [b]Injury[/b] stacks. All hits can restand airborne ragdolled opponents, and the last hit will hit all ragdolls. Hitting an opponent targeted by [b]Earthen Insect Trance[/b] will burst it and inflict its blindness effect.

This variant is, unfortunately, vastly inferior to the regular [b]Festering Strikes[/b] in neutral. Its unblockable hit takes too long to come out and bursting [b]Earthen Insect Trance[/b] hardly ever changes the outcome of using this move. Regardless, it can act as a knowledge check, but it's not worth the gamble.

The usage of this move is dealing true damage instead of [b]Injury[/b] stacks, which is useful for finishing off low-health opponents or if you'd rather let your current [b]Injury[/b] stacks drain the opponent's health without triggering a hatch. [b]Fierce Strikes[/b]'s upwards knockback makes it easier to combo into anything else ([b]Roach Swarm Explosion[/b] still not included), and it allows the user to jump and M1 the opponent midair for an extra 2 Injury stacks. While this move can restand after an uppercut, it can be somewhat strict. Doing it off of 3 M1s and skipping the uppercut can be more consistent, even if it makes you lose 3 damage.

Black Death shoots their right arm forward. Upon hitting a target, be it a player or a surface, the projectile will attach to it (and become a platform if it hit a surface); this gives the user access to [b]Reattach[/b] by pressing the move again in the next 8 seconds (the countdown will show in the move's tooltip). If more than 8 seconds pass, this move won't go on cooldown, but will be disabled for 6 seconds until the user's arm comes back. If the projectile misses, it will automatically come back to Black Death and drag all players in its way alongside it; the return angle can be modified by moving your camera to the left or right. If the opponent was being targetted by [b]Earthen Insect Trance[/b], this will also burst it.

[b]Detach[/b]'s short startup and recovery, combined with its fast projectile speed, make it an excellent poke in neutral. Landing it lets Black Death apply 2 Injury stacks and gives access to [b]Reattach[/b] (which applies 2 more Injury stacks); meanwhile the user will stay completely safe if it's blocked. If missed, be it by mistake or on purpose, it can pull the opponent in on the way back for the same benefits as [b]Reattach[/b] without the requirement to hit [b]Detach[/b] first, and the opponent will be blinded right in front of Black Death if they were targeted by [b]Earthen Insect Trance[/b] beforehand.

[b]Detach[/b] is perfect for ending combos thanks to its high speed and long range, while also guaranteeing access to [b]Reattach[/b] afterwards. [b]Reattach[/b] will will leave the opponent in a position where Black Death can potentially start a new combo altogether (even if they already spent all their cooldowns, they can still get some M1s in). However, it can sometimes be good to use this move at a close range during combos in order to allow comboing into [b]Chokehold[/b] (its unarmed variant) and Roach Swarm (any variant: regular one is easier and R variant is more optimal, aerial variant should only be used for style points or for a sneaky mixup).

Black Death retrieves their right arm back, pulling the opponent towards them if they were hit by [b]Detach[/b], disabling their ability to use M1s or skills, but [u]not stunning them[/u]. If the arm was attached to a surface, it behaves like a missed [b]Detach[/b] instead. If used on a ragdolled opponent, the move will force a wake-up if Black Death was grounded, or fling them over the user's head with true ragdoll if Black Death was airborne.

[b]Reattach[/b] plays a VERY important role in Black Death's gameplan, offering them great okizeme after finishing combos or after hitting [b]Detach[/b] in neutral. This is because it puts the opponent right in front of them and at a frame disavantage, which leaves them open for a guaranteed mixup. At the beginning, Black Death can run 50/50s with M1 or sidedash M1; they can then introduce new options such as [b]Festering Strikes[/b] to parry retaliation attempts, or [b]Roach Swarm[/b] to callout blocking once they've conditioned the opponent. They can even use [b]Chokehold[/b] as a risky option if they notice the opponent doesn't respect their pressure. If not used for okizeme, Black Death can alternatively whiff 2 or 3 M1s to prepare a downslam before pulling the opponent; adding the threat of a quick unblockable on top of the previous options (whiffing the downslam will likely get the user punished, though). In certain matchups, leaving [b]Detach[/b] on the opponent can discourage them from using long startup/recovery moves (such as Perfection's Body Repel, True Cannon's Comb or Disaster Plants's Root Swarm), as a quick pull could allow Black Death to interrupt/punish them in time.

As previously mentioned, [b]Reattach[/b] is an okizeme tool, and [i][u]NOT[/u][/i] a combo extender. They will be actionable once the pull ends. However, the 2 extra Injury stacks increase Black Death's damage output a bit. If the user would rather create some space between them and the opponent instead of going for a mixup, they can go for the airborne version to hurl them away.

Black Death's lower arms swing back before trying to grab the opponent independently from their owner; this can be done while blocking or attacking. If landed, the user will hold the opponent by the neck (interrupting any actions they were doing, if any) and slash at them, sending them far away. If blocked, the user will be interrupted and stunned for a long time. If it was landed while unarmed (from using [b]Detach[/b]), Black Death will instead punch them away, dealing regular damage instead of Injury stacks.

The ability to use [b]Chokehold[/b] while blocking makes it a looming threat in M1 trading, esentially acting as an armored attack. Alternatively, it can be used during other skills: for example, using it while the opponent tries to parry [b]Festering Strikes[/b] can catch them for a sneaky hit. The main problem with this move is how [u]incredibly unsafe on block[/u] it is. If the opponents blocks this, you will [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]explode[/color]. Because of this, Black Death should use this in neutral only a few times once they've checked that their opponent is aggresive enough to fall for it. If the opponent likes to block for longer, they're better off not using this at all and instead mixing them up with other tools.

By itself, [b]Chokehold[/b] is a great way to get a bit more damage in a combo due to it hitting ragdolled opponents and leaving Black Death fully actionable while using it and after whiffing it, which makes it really safe. It is esentially a combo ender, though; because of its big knockback and short ragdoll, the only followup available after it is [b]Detach[/b]. The only exception is if Black Death has a wall nearby, in which case they can use it to mitigate the knockback and combo into [b]Roach Swarm.[/b] Another very importart use of this move in combos is using it right after [b]Festering Strikes[/b]. This gives Black Death access to a fully unevasiveable combo if properly timed; alternatively, the threat of this option can bait the opponents' evasive by itself. It's worth mentioning that, depending on the situation, Black Death might want to use the unarmed version instead, because of it having quicker and overall higher damage than the regular version.

Black Death summons an unblockable swarm of roaches from their left side, which travels forward a moderate distance hitting players along the way. This deals extra damage the more Injury stacks the opponent has.

From a distance, [b]Roach Swarm[/b] is a quick, ranged unblockable poke that can stop aggresive opponents in their tracks if they don't look out for it; it can also grant a free hit if the opponent wastes their side dash. Its damage increases the more Injury stacks the opponent has, so it's best used after Black Death has already dealt some damage to the opponent; otherwise, they'll lose out on quite a lot of value. Besides the free damage, it will always combo into [b]Detach[/b] on hit, from any distance (this does mean that if Black Death goes for Reattach okizeme after, they won't have this move available, which makes the mixup slightly less threatening). At a close range, most notably after [b]Reattach[/b], this move becomes a very fast unblockable that can also combo into [b]Chokehold[/b]. When using Roach Swarm at a close range, look to the right as much as possible: this makes the swarm spawn closer to the opponent and hit them faster. (As long as the opponent isn't behind the user, this will work.) Roach Swarm rotation

[b]Roach Swarm[/b] is a somewhat limiting, but useful combo starter. At a close range, it can combo into [b]Chokehold[/b], then into [b]Detach[/b]. At max range it will only combo into [b]Detach[/b]. It also has two niche uses in combos: being a valid followup to [b]Fierce Strikes[/b] and comboing from [b]Chokehold[/b] with the help of a wall. In other situations, it's better to use [b]Roach Swarm Explosion[/b] for the damage and more favorable knockback. One could believe Roach Swarm can work as a crutch if they can't seem to hit fully red combos with Roach Swarm Explosion; this is not needed since it's uncounterable! Note

Pressing R during the startup of [b]Roach Swarm[/b] will cancel the projectile and make Black Death slam the roach swarm against another one, creating an unblockable and uncounterable explosion that knocks the opponent upwards and deals slightly more base damage.

Generally speaking, this variant is a worse version of [b]Roach Swarm[/b] when used in neutral: because it becomes an explosion in a set position as opposed to a projectile, it loses the close range hitbox [i]and[/i] lets the opponent dash to Black Death before the explosion happens without anything stopping them; thus, it loses both of its main uses. It can still be useful if the user is completely sure the opponent will take it or attempt to counter, as it does deal more damage than regular [b]Roach Swarm[/b].

This is where this variant shines. Its higher damage and great knockback angle allows Black Death to cash out on the opponent's Injury stacks and still continue the combo (potentially also triggering a hatch after it), increasing their damage output by a considerable amount. [b]Roach Swarm Explosion[/b] can combo out of an uppercut or a close range Detach, but won't hit on time after other moves, so the user needs to remember to route into those moves before using it.
Black Death rides the roach swarm instead of sending it as a projectile; this keeps the same properties as regular [b]Roach Swarm[/b], except for its much shorter ragdoll on hit.

[b]Aerial Roach Swarm[/b] can come in handy when Black Death wants to approach overly passive opponents: they will be hit if they try to block it, and even if the attack misses, the user remains safe while still having closed the gap between them and the opponent. Besides the extra damage from Injuries, Aerial Roach Swarm can combo into [b]Chokehold[/b] with proper timing for some cheeky damage.
[b]Aerial Roach Swarm[/b] is by no means a combo tool. Any of the other versions of [b]Roach Swarm[/b] should be used instead.

Black Death strikes a pose, before summoning two flying bugs that follow them around. Using the move again while hovering the cursor over an opponent will make them follow that opponent instead. While tracking an opponent, the bugs will position themselves in the same direction Black Death is looking at (for example, they hover behind them if looking towards the opponent, and in front of them if looking away from the opponent). When hit by an opponent, the bugs will explode, interrupting whatever attack they were doing and applying a green, blinding effect to their screen. They can also explode if hit by some of Black Death's own attacks, specifically [b]Fierce Strikes[/b] and [b]Reattach[/b] when landing from behind while not previously attached to the target but this nullifies its damage. The bugs have a tendency to get in the way of grab moves, interrupting them and bailing the user out of potential combos. Always be ready to act when this happens! No combo for you The bugs will harmlessly disappear after a period of time, or when Black Death is ragdolled.

[b]Earthen Insect Trance[/b] is a rather unconventional special, and definitely on the weaker side. However, it's far from useless. Most opponents will try to get rid of the bugs as quick as possible by hitting them directly behind them, taking the blind; but this maneuver is more dangerous the closer Black Death is to them, not only because of the blindness effect, but because it's a fraction of time they're facing directly away from the user. If Black Death can analyze this behavior properly, they can trick the opponent into getting themselves hit. On the other hand, if Black Death is certain the opponent will try to approach them with an active hitbox, they can simply look away for a moment to get the bugs in the way and stop attacks like regular front dashes or Cursed Partners's Second Wind in their tracks. Of course, the bugs also prevent certain grab moves like Honored One's Rapid Punches or Vessel's Cursed Strikes from dealing all of their damage or stun/ragdoll if not dealth with first. If all of this sounds situational... that's because it [i]is[/i]. However, it never hurts to try to use it to trick the opponent if Black Death manages to summon the bugs. At best, they'll trick them. At worst, they'll blind them and deal some chip damage without allowing the user to capitalize off of it. Overall, using this special is its own skill to master, but it's more of an extra than anything.

Black Death barely has any evasive punishable moves, so you should mainly save your evasive to avoid damage. The best way to do this is right before a hatch, usually after the Festering Strikes -> Chokehold combo. In the event that your opponent does use an evasive punishable move (Roach Swarm), you should 100% go for the punish since it isn't too hard.

Blood Manipulator has everything a great character needs, with strong neutral, great evasive bait, and high damage, allowing him to excel in nearly every situation. Supernova is the defining tool of his kit, being incredibly versatile while also having a very short cooldown. It allows him to completely shut down opponents in neutral, while also having effective applications in combos. His main, and arguably only, weakness is having to engage in M1 trades at the start of the fight to get out of Orbless Mode, but once he overcomes this obstacle, Blood Manipulator becomes unstoppable.

This is Blood Manipulator's main weakness. When in Orbless Mode (typically at the start of a fight), the main goal is getting enough awakening bar to use Convergence, since his damage and neutral are quite lackluster without it. To do this, Blood Manipulator needs to win 2 M1 trades to land the following combos, granting him enough damage to get his orbs: M1 M1 M1 Flowing Red Scale M1 M1 M1 Blood Edge In Orbless Mode, both Piercing Blood and Supernova are too risky for Blood Manipulator to use.
In neutral, both Supernova and Aerial Flowing Red Scale are very hard to play against. Blood Manipulator can abuse them to shut down the opponent and take control of the match.

Blood Manipulator's main evasive bait option is Aerial Flowing Red Scale. Using 3 M1's into this move makes it fully safe, and if positioned correctly, he can pair the orb explosion with a charged Piercing Blood to force opponents to evasive without getting a chance to punish.

The only move to watch out for is Honored One's Limitless special. it can quickly gap close and reduce the effectiveness of your Supernova's neutral game, but with quick enough reaction time you have multiple ways to counteract this: catching with M1 as he teleports, using Aerial Flowing Red Scale to negate the close range pressure, or just backdashing out. Blocking is risky as they can immediately use Rapid Punches so it's not recommended. The only other way Honored One can bypass Supernova's oppressive neutral is by interrupting the throw animation with Reversal Red + Limitless. Any followup is punishable so you dont need to worry too much about it, just be wary.

Pay special attention to Limitless usage, it's his only safe approach option so when it's on cooldown you can use Supernova unhindered. Constantly pressure with Supernova to ensure he can't ever get control of the fight. If he gets through your neutral, use Aerial Flowing Red Scale for safety and M1 trade denial.
How should you approach this matchup?

Vessel simply has no safe approach methods. His Aerial Crushing Blow and Cursed Strikes feint can be interrupted via jumping with Supernova, he cannot Manji Kick Supernova, and Divergent Fist's stun doesnt activate when Supernova is fully thrown out. If Vessel does get into melee range, Aerial Flowing Red Scale can alleviate pressure and let you get back to bullying him with Supernova.

Play passive so hes forced to engage with as many Supernova orbs as possible. Don't be afraid to use Aerial Flowing Red Scale defensively, Vessel has 85 hp so there's less pressure to get off high damage combos. Use your M1s carefully, Manji Kick is moderately effective at combo starting in M1 trades.
How should you approach this matchup?

If Vessel is an easy matchup, Restless Gambler is completely free. Little mobility and no reliable poking leaves him fully at the mercy of Supernova's consistent pressure. Door Guard can't counter it either, and he can't even get safe damage in if he does somehow win an engagement.

Zone with Supernova to make sure he can't reliably get in close. Similar to Manji Kick, it's riskier to M1 in neutral due to Door Guard so be more picky in when you want to M1 trade. M1s into Rough Energy is usually green, if you need orbs you can counter this combo for free.
How should you approach this matchup?

Perfection's only tool outside of blocking to deal with Supernova is using his Blade Mode front dash during Supernova's throw animation. None of his other abilities help in dealing with the orbs, alongside poor neutral game in general and awkward mobility. Without a counter to worry about, Aerial Flowing Red Scale can be used both defensively and as a prediction option for M1 trade denial.

More Supernova zoning. Pay attention for his Blade Mode front dash startup. If you notice slow setup M1s for a wakeup 4th M1 (such as after Stockpile or Body Repel), you can mash Supernova's counter variant for free orbs if needed, although they can predict this and not go for it.
How should you approach this matchup?

Welcome to the Character Dashboard. Here you can find general information for every character in the game. Select a character below to view their dedicated wiki page.

Crow Charmer is a Swiss Army Knife, who has tools for every situation. Every move in her kit brings unique utility to her gameplan. [i]Bird Control[/i] functions as a strong approach and M1 trading option. Her aerial front dash, [i]Flock[/i], is unique, being useful as a quick mid range combo starter that can catch opponents off guard, while also enabling mix up potential if your moves are on cooldown. [i]Spatial Transference[/i] is Crow Charmer's main combo enabler, but it also serves as a powerful mixup option and neutral tool due to its speed and low endlag. Crow Charmer’s combos are more difficult than most other characters, requiring many inputs in a short timeframe. Her moves don't ragdoll for long and the endlag on her moves when whiffed can be very high, but if you can master Crow Charmer's air combos, you'll be met with great reward in devastating damage while maintaining high amounts of safety.

Crow Charmer's neutral revolves around four main options. - Flock - Spatial Transference - Bird Control - Murmurate Flock's usability in neutral varies greatly depending on the playstyle of Crow Charmer's opponent. Against an opponent playing more defensive, she'll have less opportunities to use Flock, as it essentially becomes a front dash that can't go around the opponent. However, against more aggressive opponents, Flock can function as a way to catch side dashes towards her and punish. The opponent being aware of Flock can also make constantly jumping at midrange a viable strategy to keep them on their toes. Spatial Transference is a neutral skip, allowing Crow Charmer to instantly engage her opponent. It has less endlag than Naoya's teleport, while being less restrictive than Gojo's. Having a teleport off cooldown at midrange means Crow Charmer can teleport in front, behind, on top, or to either side of the opponent whenever she so pleases. Teleporting upwards can also be used to escape situations where Crow Charmer on the defensive without a side dash. Bird Control’s directional variants function as a one time use Divine Dogs: Totality swipe. This means Crow Charmer is entirely actionable during the start-up of the move, and does [i]not[/i] cancel upon receiving stun, although the bird will be cancelled if Crow Charmer is ragdolled. The ability to perform any movement or attack during the start-up makes Bird Control an excellent move for engaging with the opponent. Combos into anything on hit, regardless of the directional input used. But Crow Charmer can be caught by an evasive during the start-up of her follow-up attack if caught unaware. Murmurate is Crow Charmer’s most prominent neutral tool. Murmurate is extremely fast with monstrous range, often hitting way further than most expect. Crow Charmer is able to move however she like during the duration of the move, similarly to Charles' Despair or Sword-off Haruta. So despite not having any actual defensive options like blocking, the free movement makes the move far more difficult to punish. This does not mean that the move is unpublishable though, and it is still fairly risky to throw out against skilled opponents.

Evasive baiting as Crow Charmer revolves entirely around [u]mind games.[/u] Her melee moves are rarely ever punished on hit as they're all fast or send at a difficult angle. However, they [i]all[/i] have sizable endlag, a window that will open up Crow Charmer to a punish. This means, if the opponent understands how Crow Charmer plays, her options in baiting out evasive rely almost exclusively on [b]prediction.[/b] Murmurate ... Any time Crow Charmer lands Murmurate in neutral on an opponent with evasive, she creates a guessing game scenario. Murmurate R↑ R↑ after an attack is only punishable on prediction if Crow Charmer inputs a move directly after teleporting. Because the opponent has to guess whether the teleport comes out, Crow Charmer can choose to instead [i]abstain[/i] from teleporting, making them waste their evasive and setting things back to neutral. Murmurate R↑ Air Updraft Bird Control(S) Leads into another R↑ guessing game Murmurate R↑ Circling R↑ Follow ups if Crow Charmer chooses to commit to an R↑

If Crow Charmer lands M1s, it might be more beneficial to go for a true combo for quick damage instead. Requires practice to add Bird Control, otherwise simple. M1 (x3) Murmurate R↑ Bird Control(W) - optional Dive Bomb

Free Fall can steal evasives similarly to Locust Guy Wing Throw or Register Homerun. Circling has massive range and is nearly impossible to evasive punish. It is also the only restand move—moves akin to True Cannon's [i]Unsatisfied[/i] or Black Death's [i]Festering Strikes[/i]—that hits grounded opponents, making it completely safe if the first hit lands. While Impetus Updraft is fast and safe on hit, the moment its hitbox comes out, it becomes unfeintable with Spatial Transference, making it a high risk option on ragdolled opponents with evasive.

Once the opponent has wasted their evasive, Crow Charmer combo routes become extremely free. All of her moves combo into each other and out of each other. She can 1234, 2134, 4231, anything, and it will combo. M1 (x3) uppercut (surf) Bounding Dive Bomb R↑ Bounding Bird Control(S) Murmurate (surf) Bounding R↓ Impetus Updraft (use twice) Far more difficult on dummies than it is on players due to how dummies have zero ping and interact differently with uppercut surfing. Note This is the highest damaging combo Crow Charmer can perform that doesn't use any of her techs. Fills opponent's evasive bar after the last swing of Impetus. It may be worth going for this combo if Crow Charmer's opponent has [i]just[/i] evasived. A single strong combo like this is not main draw of Crow Charmer. Her true strength within her combos comes from the sheer amount of routes she has to offer. Leads into an extremely safe finish within -> Bird Control and Murmurate Impetus Updraft (use twice) R(w) Circling ... Easy combo that can easily catch people off guard due to its speed Impetus Updraft R↑ Dive Bomb ... Out of M1s, Circling can be charged to yellow, giving her more conversion options M1 (x3) Circling ... Extremely stylish combo that can convert into a high area Dive Bomb ... Bounding Bird Control(W) Air Updraft Free Fall ... Circling can combo into Impetus without a teleport, by changing the direction of Circling's knockback Circling side dash Impetus Updraft Mentioned because Impetus Updraft's only true follow up is Murmurate Impetus Updraft (use twice) Murmurate ...and there's far more Crow Charmer has to offer within combos, but those are self-explanatory. Crow Charmer's best neutral option is Murmurate, and that'll combo into any one of her other grounded moves. She has some of the most combo freedom within JJS.

Because of the very small ragdoll duration of a lot of Crow Charmer's moves, green combos become more of a boon than a flaw, something she can take advantage of when moves are on cooldown. Crow Charmer has some of the longest cooldowns in the game. Combine that with short cooldowns, and sometimes it can feel as though Crow Charmer has nothing to do after landing a hit. Fortunately, she can get around that hurdle by utilizing Bounding. M1 (x3) Uppercut (surf) Bounding ... Bounding is completely safe on hit and launches Crow Charmer directly above the opponent. The opponent stalls in the air and exits ragdoll while she is [i]still[/i] airborne, letting her come down in an attempt to get another M1 combo. This is a mix up opportunity that Crow Charmer gains access to every time she lands a Bounding. She can land on top of the opponent and ride them on the way down. She can land before the opponent does, roll, and side dash to get around their block that way. She react and dash in the direction the opponent dashes to catch them. Crow Charmer has a whole conrucopia of options available to her after Bounding lands. These Bounding loops can singlehandedly win her fights. Alongside the Bounding mixup, there are some other green combos she has access to. Jump on the opponent's head Flock M1s ... This might cause an M1 trade, but often times the opponent is simply not ready for this Impetus Updraft (use twice) (Aim the second hit away) M1s ... First hit of Murmurate has no ragdoll time once the opponent touches the ground. First hit of Murmurate M1s ... Usually happens on accident, but Crow Charmer can capitalize if it happens. Note
Green Combos and the Bounding Mixup

Umbilical cord is a way to stack moves with other moves, duplicate moves, open up new follow ups to other moves, and apply extreme pressure in neutral. While it takes away your main m1 trading tool, being bird control, it makes up for it by adding egregious amounts of damage. Bilicing my FUCKING cord so FUCKING hard rn

TECH HOW WHY ITS USEFUL DELAY BOUNCE M1X4 UPPER, R, Q, 4+W, 3. Using this tech makes any combo coming off of it unpunishable. By using forward bird control, and sky high, it delays the upwards momentum until they hit the ground again. You can combine this with any move following it, and even if they evasive, as soon as they hit the ground they will be ragdolled.
Crow Charmer’s fourth M1 is extremely slow and easy to punish compared to other characters. Never use this over uppercut. Or in general. There’s no point.
Crow Charmer’s Uppercut launches the opponent much higher than usual.

Crow Charmer quickly swings her axe upwards, launching opponents into the air. This move cannot be cancelled with [i]Spatial Transference[/i] if you miss the swing. Fast startup with a very large upwards hitbox, but leaves a lot to be desired horizontally and downwards. This means just a tiny bit of rubble can completely mess up Crow Charmer's combo. With Impetus also having some of the highest [noauto]whiff endlag[/noauto] of any base attacking move, Crow Charmer will need to be very wary of how and when she uses this attack against an enemy. The endlag also makes it a poor option in M1 trading. As well as the fact that Crow Charmer cannot feint after the hitbox comes out. Impetus Updraft is unpunishable on hit when used out of M1s. It's technically punishable on hit on a ragdolled enemy and on reaction, but it is very rare for an opponent to be able to do this to Crow Charmer consistently. An opponent who knows how to face her will likely choose to save their evasive for more useful areas, like predicting an upwards Spatial Transference. Quick combo that will catch those who are not ready to evasive punish the teleport. m1s (x3) Impetus Updraft R↑ Dive Bomb ... Additionally, with correct positioning on a ragdolled opponent, Crow Charmer can surf and lead into a Bounding [i]without[/i] the use of a Spatial Transference. Useful, if she wants to go into some Bounding loops. Overall, single-use Impetus Updraft finds itself to be much [i]less[/i] valuable to the Crow Charmer gameplan than Air Updraft or double-use Impetus.

Crow Charmer swings her axe and additional two times, the first juggling while the second knocks them away. It's fairly high damage makes it great in combos, however it's main flaw is the fact it has trouble linking into max height [i]Dive-Bomb[/i] due to it sacrificing [i]Air Updraft[/i]. Unlike single-use Impetus, this move can be cancelled with a Spatial Transference [i]after[/i] the hitbox comes out, letting Crow Charmer bail out of it to bait evasive, or reposition entirely for another interaction.

Double use [i]Impetus Updraft[/i] can be extended with after any move in her kit. Other than [i]Flock[/i] and [i]Bounding[/i], they're all extremely consistent to combo afterwards. Comboing [b]after[/b] double use [i]Impetus Updraft[/i] can be done with [i]Spatial Transference↑[/i]. After using the teleport, Circling (or [color=#ffdf00]Yellow[/color]) and Murmurate are amazing follow ups. Another follow up it has that's rather precise is [i]Flock[/i]. By teleporting, jumping, and immediately using [i]Flock[/i], she can land the grab portion and immediately follow up with [i]Dive-bomb[/i].

Crow Charmer[color=hsl(233, 39%, 23%)][/color] swings her axe in a diagonal arc, hitting any opponent above her and knocking them in a arc. During the swing, the move cannot be feinted with [i]Spatial Transference[/i] unless it hits anyone. Due to it's nature as an air exclusive move, as long as it's fairly unwelcoming hitbox, it's exclusively a combo extender. However, by no means is it a bad one. By using it, [color=hsl(233, 39%, 23%)]Crow Charmer[/color] able to consistently link with other moves via the use of [i]Flock[/i], and creates a path to use max height [i]Dive-Bomb[/i]. On top of that, it has extremely low punishability due to it's fast [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]startup[/color] and high knockback.

[i]Air Updraft[/i] is an amazing combo extender, due to how easily it links into other moves as well as it's ability to achieve max height [i]Dive-Bomb[/i]. This key factor allows it to surpass grounded combo routes. Following up with [i]Air Updraft[/i] is possible after an uppercut, [i]Dive-Bomb[/i], [i]Bird Control(W)[/i], and sometimes [i]Murmurate[/i]. Extending after [i]Murmurate[/i] requires the ragdolled player to be hit higher, because if it's used when they're too low it'll whiff. It's advised to stick to using the former 3 options. Follow ups after [i]Air Updraft[/i] are capable of is [i]Flock[/i] and [i]Murmurate[/i]. Both of these require the usage of [i]Spatial Transference(W)[/i].

Crow Charmer performs 2 large swings with her axe. This move can be charged to 3 distinct levels. [b]Uncharged[/b]: Both swings are blockable. The second swing will launch the opponent far forward. [b]Partially Charged[/b] ([color=#fffd00]Yellow [/color]Outline): The second swing becomes unblockable. The second swing will launch the opponent straight upwards. [b]Fully Charged[/b] ([color=#ff0000]Red[/color] Outline): Both swings become unblockable. The second swing will launch the opponent straight upwards like the partially charged version. This move cannot be cancelled with [i]Spatial Transference[/i] once the second swing comes out, unless it hits the opponent.

Combo starting with [i]Circling[/i] is fairly risky. Its high speed and large hitbox make up for it being blockable, but extremely committal on whiff or block. When approaching with [i]Circling[/i], charging the attack varies upon opponent. If they can't punish it in between swings, charging to yellow is recommended. Comboing after [i]Circling[/i] is simple. No charge allows you to follow up with [i]Spatial Transference (Forward)[/i], then most consistently [i]Murmurate[/i] or [i]Bird Control(S)[/i]. While the charged version can be followed up using nearly anything.

[i]Circling[/i] is best used after a downslam, uppercut, or 3 M1s. By using downslams and uppercuts, it gives Crow Charmer more time to charge to the other variants of the move. The most she can charge [i]Circling[/i] after 3 M1s is to the yellow charge, immediately allowing a air combo follow up. [i]Circling[/i] can fit anywhere in any combo due to it hitting ground and leading into other moves seamlessly.

Crow Charmer flies forward, grabbing her opponent with her axe before slamming down into the ground. Then, the opponent is knocked up vertically. The damage of the slam increases when it falls a far enough distance. This move cannot be cancelled using [i]Spatial Transference[/i]. The grab hitbox of [i]Dive-Bomb[/i] is immensely large, making it extremely consistent for air combos/follow ups. This move is entirely uncancelable via [i]Spaital Transference[/i].

While being fairly minor, [i]Dive-Bomb[/i]'s initial grab can be used at a lower range after something such as a headtap, [i]Spatial Transference[/i], or [i]Bird Control[/i]. In the case of Crow Charmer whiffing this move, attempt to turn around with the initial forward velocity and avoid someone's block. This greatly reduces it's punishability.

[i]Dive-Bomb[/i] combos flawlessly after all of her moves. After [i]Air Updraft[/i] she can do R↑, [i]Flock[/i]. After which, [i]Dive-Bomb[/i] will get it's max height. It can also be done after [i]Bird Control↑[/i], Murmurate, single use [i]Impetus Updraft[/i], [i]Bounding[/i], and [i]Flock[/i]. All of which requiring [i]Spatial Transference[/i] to be used first. Comboing after the move is done by either waiting for them to fall, or using [i]Spatial Transference[/i] to follow up with [i]Flock/Bounding[/i] or [i]Air Updraft[/i].

Crow Charmer throws her axe in a circle around her. This move can hit up to two times, and the first hit has true ragdoll. Crow Charmer can move freely during this move, similar to Aspiring Mangaka's [i]Despair[/i]. If used mid-air, Crow Charmer will be stalled in the air until the move ends and will not be able to move freely. This move cannot be canceled with [i]Spatial Transference[/i] on specifically block.

[i]Murmurate[/i] is byfar the best move for neutral in Crow Charmer's kit. Its extreme speed and range make it a powerful prediction tool, as well as an amazing call out tool. As well as that, it's an incredibly safe poke as long as the user keeps a safe distance. This is best done by positioning oneself and poking with [i]Murmurate[/i]'s longest hitbox, then immediately S keying if blocked. On hit from a far range, it can immediately be canceled with [i]Spatial Transference[/i], allowing Crow Charmer to immediately follow up with the true ragdoll by using another move. This is best done by using [i]Spatial Transference↑[/i], then [i]Impetus Updraft[/i] or [i]Circling[/i] ([color=#ffcc00]Yellow[/color]) Similar to the previous on hit, hitting it close range allows you to use [i]Spatial Transference[/i] to follow up with [i]Dive-Bomb[/i] or [i]Bounding[/i]. Air updraft however is fairly inconsistent.

Byfar, this move is amazing at catching her rather high knockback moves. Meaning [i]Circling[/i] and double use [i]Impetus Updraft[/i]. It can also catch [i]Air Updraft[/i]'s knockback, but requires [i]Spatial Transference↑[/i] to be used first. As previously mentioned, follow ups after this move are done with [i]Spatial Transference[/i]. After using its forward variant, [i]Circling[/i] and [i]Impetus Updraft[/i] is most consistent. After using its neutral variant, [i]Dive-Bomb[/i] and [i]Bounding[/i] is most consistent

Crow Charmer stalls in the air and slams down with her axe, launching opponents straight into the ground. Upon hitting the ground, the opponent will be bounced back up to Crow Charmer's elevation. Activates when using [i]Murmurate[/i] above a certain height threshold, slightly higher than [i]Spatial Transference[/i]. Due to how the move is coded, it flings anyone hit by it that's above the JJS map. This means it affects any map in ranked other than the grasslands.

[i]Freefall[/i] is fairly specific. It's conditions can't be fulfilled all that easily compared to her other moves. However, it can be used after bounding in most cases. Usually after [i]Circling[/I] ([color=#ff0000]Red[/color] or [color=#ffdf00]Yellow[/color] charge), [i]Dive-Bomb[/i], single use [i]Impetus Updraft[/i], and uppercut. All of which possible after [i]Spatial Transference[/i]. Comboing after is fairly simple. Just by using [i]Spatial Transference[/i], Crow Charmer can immediately go back down to follow up with any move. If she wants to continue it midair, [i]Dive-Bomb[/i] is most consistent. She can also movestack with [i]Bird Control↑/↓[/i] to make follow ups easier. If downslam bird is used, she can immediately teleport downwards to quickly follow up.
For Crow Charmer, this move is rarely used due to the fact it's both unoptimal damage wise and has fairly unfavorable knockback. It's mostly delegated to style.

Crow Charmer grabs onto a crow and uses it to hover in the air for a short time before letting go of it. If used again, the move will cancel early. If Crow Charmer cancels the move during the flight using [i]Spatial Transference[/i], Bird Control will not be put on cooldown and can be used again. The move can be used again if a directional variant (↑/↓) is used, causing it to then lock onto a selected target. Evil things occur if you immediately feint this move.

This moves neutral application is entirely dependent on the users ability to approach with M1s. By using it to mixup her landing in various ways as mentioned above, its essentially a mind game for whoever the Crow Charmer is fighting. If disengaging or repositioning, it's advised to feint it to replenish itss cooldown. If approaching, it's advised to at some point cancel the bird early by locking it onto a opponent.

Crow Charmer calls a bird to attack the player she's targeting with her cursor. Crow Charmer can act freely during this move and the bird will not disappear if she is stunned, only if she is ragdolled. If Crow Charmer is moving forwards, the bird will launch the opponent upwards and not hit grounded ragdoll. This move will swarm around a grabbed player, most notably from [i]Bounding[/i] or [i]Dive-Bomb[/i]. This move can only hit upwards ragdoll. Its ragdoll time is set, similar to bounding.

[i]Bird-Control↑[/i] is an amazing M1 trading tool. Due to the fact it still triggers if Crow charmer is stunned after its use, being extra block pressure, and the fact it allows her to get out of bad/disadvantageous situations. It's far better to use in neutral over [i]Bird Control↓[/i] due to the fact that, on hit, it replenishes R special.

Due to the fact it can't hit grounded ragdoll, its combo potential is heavily limited. However, it's possible to use after an uppercut or bounding. If Crow Charmer uses [i]Bird Control↑[/i] before a move, it allows it to seamlessly connect.

Crow Charmer calls a bird to attack the player she's targeting with her cursor. Crow Charmer can act freely during this move and the bird will not disappear if she is stunned, only if she is ragdolled. If Crow Charmer is moving backwards, the bird will launch the opponent downwards. This move will swarm around a grabbed player, most notably from [i]Bounding[/i] or [i]Dive-Bomb[/i].
Same benefits as [i]Bird Control↑[/i], however, it not replenishing R special as well as its less favorable ragdoll duration makes it notably less viable.

Extremely crucial combo tool that allows her to quicken combos and fit more damage into them. Since all of her moves hit on grounded, it never hurts to use in the middle of one. As with [i]Bird Control↑[/i], it allows her to movestack the bird into other skills. As long as it's used before the follow up. The best use case of this is with [i]Dive-Bomb[/i], allowing her to immediately hit the opponent as soon as the skill ends.

Crow Charmer calls her brother to use his cursed technique to teleport her in a direction. She can teleport forwards, backwards, left, or right depending on which direction she is moving when she uses the move. If she uses [i]Spatial Transference[/i] while not holding any directional button she will teleport upwards into the air if she is on the ground, and downwards onto the ground if she is in the air. Crow Charmer can cancel any of her moves into [i]Spatial Transference[/i] (with exceptions, written in each moves description) until they are blocked. When Crow Charmer lands any move (except Bounding and backwards Bird Control), this move will be taken off cooldown. Due to these properties, [i]Spatial Transference[/i] is what enables most of Crow Charmer's air combos. It is also a potent mixup option due to its fast speed and ambiguity.

Cursed Partners main gimmick are fast dash moves with supreme block pressure, along with good defense via [i]Outburst[/i] (Parry) and [i]Rika Haymaker[/i], allowing him to be extremely aggressive while maintaining safety. Combined with [i]Resolute Slash[/i] as a ranged block bypass, Cursed Partners has a solution for almost any situation he finds himself in. Rika is an extremely effective assist moveset, working as a combo tool, evasive bait, movement/approach tool and as a reversal. Additionally, having 5 moves along with decent cooldowns allows Cursed Partners to keep pressing the advantage and/or have tools constantly (15,15,16,16) (10 for rika). Cursed Partners is a great pick for offense up close while also having good versatilities in Rika to cover weaknesses.

Cursed Partners excels at shutting down aggressive opponents while also being a decent rushdown himself. [i]Veilstep[/i], [i]Rika Smash[/i] and [i]Second Wind[/i] are reliable for catching opponents off guard, [i]Rika Smash[/i], [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] and [i]Outburst[/i] assures Yuta has good defensive options while [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] and [i]Resolute Slash[/i] enables him to get the offense on blocking opponents.

You can also use Rika Smash (Aerial) on any uptilt move (e.g: Veilstep) 3 m1s Severing Path Rika Smash (aerial) Since [i]Rika Smash[/i] (Aerial) applies true ragdoll and converts into both heavy hitting moves ([i]Resolute Slash[/i], [i]Outburst[/i] (Max charge)), additionally falling on a low cooldown (10s), while also being near instantaneous, your opponent will always have to evasive right after any uptilt move or suffer tremendous damage. [i]Rika Smash[/i] (Aerial) will also slow your opponent down substantiallly if they do evasive, potentially allowing for mixups if they do evasive. 3m1s Resolute slash rikahaymaker veilstep Normally [i]Resolute Slash[/i] is evasive punishable, but if you use [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] after they've been knocked back, it follows them if they try to punish you, which can lead into [i]Veilstep[/i]. Even if they don't evasive, they'll still eat [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] into [i]Veilstep[/i]. On block, [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] does 18 damage and just pushes them back instead of ragdolling which could lead to a untrue mixup.

Cursed Partners combos deal a moderate amount of damage most of the time, potentially insane damage if his variants are used properly and with some sneaky M1s in. 3 M1s Severing path Uppercut Rika Smash (Aerial) Outburst (max charge) Second Wind Resolute Slash (Black flash) A simple, safe yet effective combo, you can sneak in a downslam after [i]Rika Smash[/i] (Aerial) if you are sure the opponent doesn't have their evasive, this combo acts as both evasive bait and well, a combo. Veilstep Rika Smash (Aerial) Outburst (Max charge) second wind resolute slash (black flash) Cursed Partners safe combo for converting off of his neutral option [i]Veilstep[/i], which can be interchangeable with [i]Second Wind[/i]. 3 m1s Uppercut Severing Path (Aerial) Outburst (max charge) Second Wind Rika Haymaker Resolute Slash (BLACK FLASH) This is Cursed Partners main combo after baiting evasive, [i]Severing Path[/i] (Aerial) deals 4 more damage than normal [i]Severing Path[/i], using up a [i]Second Wind[/i] charge but doesn't put [i]Second Wind[/i] on cooldown if you have yet to use your first charge, allowing you to use [i]Second Wind[/i] again. The timing for both [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] and [i]Resolute Slash[/i] to hit can be tricky, but you can avoid this by using [i]Rika Smash[/i], exchanging 2 damage for consistency.

Cursed Partners is one of the buggier characters as of current, having plenty of issues with his moves as follow: - [i]Second Wind[/i] sometimes teleports the opponent after slamming them, this becomes ever more apparent as the move does not mesh well with the destruction physics, making it extremely difficult for, or even incapacitating Yuta from following-up. - The destruction physics can also sometimes reduce the ragdoll duration of Cursed Partners moves if your opponent is beneath debris. - Rika's move slots can become invisible sometimes. Rika gets put on a 6 second cooldown if [i]Rika Launch[/i]'s feint variant was activated. Do an M1 or dash and then [i]Rika Launch[/i] to avoid getting put on a 13 second cooldown. Ever since [i]Outburst[/i]'s initial slash has been changed to hit grounded ragdolls, the move can be charged up to max after [i]Severing Path[/i] and [i]Second wind[/i], and charged up to 2 after [i]Resolute Slash[/i]. [i]Outburst[/i] has a very small parry window (0.2 seconds, which is very short). But Cursed Partners is incentivised by a 2 second cooldown reduction on Rika, and this variant can be useful against mixups or certain moves that are hard to dodge, especially if dashes are unavailable.

Severing Path is exclusively Cursed Partners main convert/extender for his combos, being unreliable in neutral or mixups due to its decently slow startup along with a generously long recovery time. Don't use it on a ragdolled player if they have their evasive since the startup is reactable. Jump after landing this move if you want to follow up with Second Wind to make it safer and more consistent. Severing Path could also be used as an M1 reset when paired with Rika Launch (Grounded) to cancel the move before the final ragdolling strike. Be careful as the timing required to pull this off is extremely unintuitive.

Backwards Severing Path, otherwise known as Veilstep, stand at the pinnacle of Cursed Partners neutral, providing Melee I-frames, low startup and a moving, lingering hitbox. Being essentially unpunishable, Veilstep provides exceptional block pressure as a poke tool. This move can also be used to avoid getting evasive punished, rather than the normal variant of Severing Path. It's recommended to save this move in neutral against certain opponents (ex. Vessel/Head of the Hei) due to the melee iframes and knock-up that can combo into Rika Downslam.

Resolute Slash is really good to punish wasted side dashes from a close-medium distance, and can also be useful when done on wake-up as the startup and windup are pretty fast, coupled with the fact that the only way to deal with a wake-up Resolute Slash is to either evasive or use a counter. While the Black Flash variant is what most people would use, the regular variant has the unique effect of keeping the enemy ragdolled longer, meaning Cursed Partners can extend this into either 1 or 3 if Resolute Slash hits. Both of these moves can be feinted out of to remove the endlag.

This variant is mostly useful for the end of a combo, as the knockback sends the opponent out of side dash range while also waking them up once the knockback is done. Unlike Resolute Slash, this move can be used against ragdolled opponents, which is the reason why most players use this variant instead. Ironically, this variant does NOT deal more damage than its base move, despite being a Black Flash. The only difference it has is that it hits grounded ragdolls at the cost of being punishable on whiff (and having a really cool finisher. It can also be feinted to remove its long endlag).

Outburst is a really safe move; using it in M1 trades or when you know you're about to get hit basically guarantees your safety since it will either hit the parry or the explosion. It can also be used to parry projectiles. If you want to use the fully charged variant in a combo but you know the opponent won't be ragdolled for enough time to land it, you can use Rika Smash during the windup to extend their ragdoll (pairing these 2 moves together is also really good evasive bait, but you're putting your best moves on cooldown for it).

The first use of Second Wind is punishable in neutral, but it's a very small window, so if they're not expecting it, you can get away with it. Second Wind also has a really good vertical hitbox. Pair that with it having melee iframes you can cancel a lot of aerial and grounded moves (ex. Crushing Blow, Cursed Strikes, and Speed Crash) by doing Jump + 4. If you don't land the first use, save the second one for combos (and if you miss the second one make sure to feint to remove endlag).
This move does 15 damage, leads into all of his moves (including a downslam) at the cost of taking up both 4 and 1 if used, and requires an enemy to be in front of you to use it.

Rika Smash is a good tool for punishing opponents trying to get an advantage out of your own mistakes. It forces the opponent to block, so it's useful in M1 trades. It can combo into and out of every move in your kit, you can also use it with Outburst, like mentioned earlier.

FEINT Rika launch is good for movement and canceling due to it's feinting ability, it's regular cooldown is 10s but if feinted with a move, it turns into a 6s cooldown, so always do a jump m1 or a forward/side dash for optimal cooldowns with movement. Feinting is really useful to cancel the endlag of heavy moves like both of Resolute Slash variants, and the 2nd part of Second Wind.

AERIAL FEINT This variant has the same cooldown propreties as the first, but with the difference being vertical moviment instead of horizontal, giving you easy acess to the air. Gaining height like this is useful for some things, like easy acess to rolls, dodging a move or just being unpredictable with your moviment. However, its value is easily overshadowed by the normal variant, thanks to the acess of the m1 reset previously mentioned, and the fact that horizontal moviment has more uses in a fight, and is harder to react.

Rika Haymaker is the best evasive baiting tool Rika has. You can use it in neutral to guarantee your safety while it's active, and because of it's slow windup rika follows people if they evasive (and timed well) which can lead to another combo after you caught them. it does 18 damage instead of the usual 12 when blocked and instead of knocking them back just pushes them which can lead to a silly mixup.

Cursed Partners has slightly better neutral, slightly better combo damage. While Honored One cannot reliably use [i]Lapse Blue[/i] for evasive bait, considering they potentially cannot go for [i]Lapse Blue[/i] > Special > [i]Rapid Punches[/i] / M1s due to Cursed Partners's Parry. Veilstep may be useful if the Honored One has shown a preference for teleporting. Truly nothing is notable about this matchup other than the potential denial of one of Honored One's most effective combo paths. Additionally, please don't try to Parry [i]Reversal Red[/i]. It hasn't exploded yet.

Cursed Partners has better neutral, combo damage, evasive bait, a defensive parry that is useful against green mixups, with overall more utility. If Vessel uses the aerial variants of [i]Cursed Strikes[/i] and [i]Crushing Blow[/i] for mobility, [i]Second Wind[/i] can catch them midair. You may even cancel their move and put it on cooldown before they can feint the move. Beware of [i]Manji KIck[/i], as it can both counter Rika and may be able to capitalize off of Cursed Partners failing the [i]Severing Path[/i] M1 reset. It also can be used to counter 3 M1s [i]Resolute Slash[/i] as there is a sliver of green, so be mindful with combo paths.

Blood Manipulator's [i]Supernova[/i] move is considered as explosion type damage, meaning that most counter moves and counter-esque like Cursed Partners' [i]Outburst[/i] parry will not counter it, meaning that one of Cursed Partners main defensive tools will not work. However, this does not mean counterplay to Blood Manipulator is non-existent. [i]Second Wind[/i]'s windup speed is one of the only moves that can rival the speed in which a [i]Supernova[/i] comes out, and there are movement tools like [i]Veilstep, Resolute Slash[/i]'s teleport, and [i]Rika launch[/i] that can close the gap against a supernova. With all of the mentioned, the matchup into Blood Manipulator is more close to an extreme disadvantage than a regular disadvantage because of how strong [i]Supernova[/i] would be if the enemy adopts a more passive playstyle to try and guarantee the effect of [i]Supernova[/i], and how [i]Flowing Red Scales Air Variant[/i] can deny most of the engagement attempts from Rushdown Characters, which Cursed Partners is. This fight will (usually) not be anime accurate.

Like every other mirror matchup, you and your opponent are both equal, with no advantage. Some important things to note (if you find yourself in the Cursed Partners Mirror), is that [i]Outburst's[/i] parry variant can counter all of your base moves with the exception of the [i]Outburst[/i] Explosion. [i]Second wind[/i] is also useful if your enemy uses the [i]Rika Launch Air variant[/i] since you can use it to catch them midair similar to other air moves in the game. But in the end, the better player will always win.
Cursed Partners has better combo damage, neutral, evasive bait, true combos, and a defensive parry. (will expand later too lazy rn)

Cursed Partners has better combo damage, neutral, and evasive bait than Salaryman. [i]Outburst[/i] is especially useful in this matchup due to the Parry. Salaryman relies on easily parriable moves in neutral, utilizing usually non-threatening combos without green mixups, in which case the Parry is particularly useful. Be mindful of being caught without [i]Outburst[/i], and not to let Salaryman to interrupt and debuff you. Watch for Salaryman's [i]Severance Kick (Backward)[/i] when playing aggressively as it grants an m1 reset on interruption.

A strong M1-centric rushdown augmented with some of the fastest mobility in the game, Defense Attorney excels at tripping his opponents up with his blistering speed, making them second-guess themselves at every turn with his strong mix-up game. Defense Attorney has a pretty good neutral game relative to other M1 merchants, with 3+R and R+R on top of your regular side dash and front-dash, making his movement way faster than most characters. He also has access to multiple incredibly strong pokes, with two safe pokes in 3 and R+4, and an unsafe but guardbreaking poke in R+3. His ultimate allows him to continue piling on the pressure, either through confiscation or through his awakening. Defense Attorney is a great pick for enhancing and making use of well-developed fundamentals.

Strategy with Defense Attorney starts with you trying to get up close with your mobility tools to net you an M1 string and a knockdown, so you can start your offense. Once you put an opponent in a ragdoll state, Defense Attorney becomes a much more dangerous threat, with his ability to control when ragdoll ends with his special [url=#sec-no-escape-2][b][b]No Escape[/b][/b][/url] ( [b]R[/b] ). With his gavel out of the way, he gains access to answers to just about any option an opponent might throw out. Your goal is to pick up on habits and respond accordingly, capitalizing on reads to cash out damage, and to keep changing things up until your opponent is suffocated in your pressure.

Typically, [b][url=#sec-no-escape-2]No Escape[/url][/b] ([b]R + R [/b]) is what you would prefer to open with at almost all ranges, as Defense Attorney lets you manipulate your velocity on the hop by holding jump or a movement key, or even both. Here are some examples: Sends you further R Spacebar + w r (instantly) Hops a short distance R S R (INSTANTLY)

Although [b][b][url=#sec-judgement-s-reach]Judgement's Reach[/url][/b][/b] [b][b]3 + R [/b][/b] variant is less versatile than R + R in terms of movement and approach options, it remains a valuable tool thanks to its built-in mix-up. Unlike other gavel-dependent options, it does not put your gavel on cooldown. [b][b]3 + R[/b][/b] can also be used mid-air, allowing you to combine it with other approach options to cover even greater distances. There are two main ways to use Defense Attorney's 3 + R: [b][b]Approaching[/b][/b]: Use it to close the distance and initiate offense. [b][b] Post-knockdown pressure[/b][/b]: Use it after a knockdown to threaten either 3's interruption variant or 3 + 3, forcing your opponent to respect the mixup.

[b][url=#sec-pressing-charges]Pressing Charges[/url][/b] is an unusual option that is **highly vulnerable to interruption**. Most moves can hit you out of it, with a few exceptions, such as Cursed Strikes and Cleaving Whirlwind. This is because [b][url=#sec-pressing-charges-kick]Pressing Charges[/url][/b] produces a hitbox during the initial portion of the move. Despite this weakness, unpredictability is what makes [url=#sec-pressing-charges]Pressing Charges[/url] effective. Its variants can respectively [b]crush actions[/b] and [b]block attacks[/b], allowing Defense Attorney to catch opponents off guard. [i]Use this option sparingly.[/i] A whiff leaves you in a highly disadvantageous position.
Pressing Charges+ Any Variant  ( The Most Commital )

Defense Attorney's combo routes are pretty easy to [i]"grapple"[/i]. He can combo pretty much anything in his kit into and out of another thing in his kit, but here's a few combos that you should know. Starting with Defense Attorney's bread and butter:

3 m1s uppercut R (whiff) 4 FrontDash 2 m1s uppercut 1 2 3 R R (optional) Defense Attorney's main BNB. Solid damage, sets up mix at the end with R, and can lead to an m1 reset if you play your cards right. If your opponent doesn't have evasive, you'll be using this combo on them a vast majority of the time. Defense Attorney doesn't have much in the way of actual true combos. The most you can do is 3 m1s into Extended Swings, which is pretty lackluster. Defense Attorney does, however, have safe evasive bait that leads into decent damage; when they do have evasive, use this one instead. 3 m1s 2 backdash + 3 r (whiff) sidedash + 4 frontdash 2 m1s 1 Justice Served into Grapple is the safest way Defense Attorney can bait evasive, so while this combo may not be true, it's a pretty safe way to either deal a load of damage or bait evasive. Bear in mind that this combo doesn't provide any mix afterwards, as your R will be on cooldown.

Defense Attorney's gavel-less move variants are generally faster than their standard counterparts, making them useful for situations such as resets, oki, and blockbreaking. However, using these variants normally puts his innate, [b][b][url=#sec-no-escape-2]No Escape[/url][/b][/b], on cooldown. This drawback can be [b]bypassed[/b] by exploiting No Escape's feint mechanics. By inputting another move before the feint window closes, you can perform a gavel-less variant without putting No Escape on cooldown. The only exception is [u][url=#sec-pressing-charges]Pressing Charges[/url][/u], which cannot be used to trigger this interaction.

Your main combo ender. You can confirm it off of m1s, uppercut, and Justice Served when timed right. It's somewhat quick and large enough to use in neutral to catch someone off-guard, but it's also pretty easily punishable on block... Yeah just stick to using this as combo food. It's also a surprisingly common misconception that you can immediately evasive and punish the endlag of this move on hit. You can't. This move is safe. It also has a very high tendency to drop at specific ranges or when debris interferes, so keep this in mind (you can even see this in the GIF of the move shown above).

[i]This [/i]move is what's basically the backbone of Defense Attorney's mix. Melee invul, huge, incredibly quick, even hits people who aren't blocking it, and most importantly crushes on block AND interruption, this move is insane. This move alone makes opponents wary when your mallet is thrown out, and forces them to stop what they're doing. But this doesn't mean that you should [i]always[/i] use this move once your mallet is out. A large, common mistake that I see in novice Defense Attorney players is CONSTANTLY using this sweep. Reason being that against newer players, this move is seemingly no risk as it knocks back even when it doesn't crush. But that knockback has no stun (and damage, but that's kind of a non-issue) on it; a more experienced player will sometimes catch you on hit and punish the endlag. Like a majority of Defense Attorney's kit, you should use this move carefully to form and/or punish habits. Note when the opponent tends to throw out moves, and use R+1 to punish them.

A coward would call this move mere combo food. A player without conviction... A player without drive to be... [i]more...[/i] Sure you can use it during your combos. It's probably the most safe option you have after m1s and you can use Grapple right after to get pretty safe damage when your opponent has evasive, and when they don't you can combo out of it with R+4 or 1... But what about using this move... [i]unsafely...[/i] This move has the benefit of being pretty big and lagless for a guard-breaking move, meaning that you can surprisingly get away with using this move raw quite often. A big reason why is because people aren't typically that concerned about getting their guard broken by moves on other characters, as they typically don't lead to true combos and tend to be evasive-able. Justice Served, however, has the benefit of crushing blocks and leading straight into an m1 chain. A lot of the time this means that you can get away with throwing out side dash + Justice Served raw, and since the usual reaction to a close quarters side dash is to block the obvious incoming m1... you see where this is going. This is, of course, unsafe. Sure, Justice Served has comparatively low windup and endlag compared to similar guardbreaks, but it's still plenty punishable on whiff/reaction. But a lot of Defense Attorney's gameplan is messing with your opponents head and trying to get them to pick up bad habits in an attempt to counterplay you. Hitting someone with raw Justice Served multiple times may cause them to adopt bad habits against you, like retreating after you side dash at them, or trying to stuff out the supposed incoming Justice Served with m1s on reaction to your side dash. You shouldn't spam raw Justice Served. You also shouldn't forget that it's still plenty useful as combo food as well, converting off of ragdolls and into every move in Defense Attorney's kit. But when it works... [i]hoooooooooooooo boy[/i] it works. Justice Served tends to sometimes whiff at close range or when debris is at play. Judgement's Reach is a very interesting move. It's the biggest disjoint in your kit, and you're going to be using it as such; it's a solid poke to use in neutral when fishing for a hit. What makes this move interesting is the interruption property that it has; if this move lands on someone who's in the process of using a move/m1s (unless that move is a counter, of course), it'll inflict a long period of stun on that player, allowing for a follow-up with a front dash. Bear in mind that landing the interruption doesn't reset your front dash cooldown, so sometimes you'll have to settle for a side dash and m1 to convert. You can also situationally land punishes after an evasive that would be hard to do with normal m1s; for example, Restless Gambler's main bnb (Uppercut Surf > Fever Breaker) is hard to punish normally with m1s. Judgement's Reach can easily punish the Restless Gambler after the uppercut, catching them while they're using Fever Breaker, and netting you a combo. Another good example is True Cannon's Appetizer; a True Cannon player may think that they're safe attepting to combo extend out of that move from a distance, but typically you can easily catch them with Judgement's Reach due to how long that move's duration is. Even if you don't land the interruption variant and just land the normal first hit, you can side dash immediately and go in for an m1 string. This can catch players off guard (especially against a wall) and lead to huge damage. All in all, Judgement's Reach is a great yet situational poke that has its place in Defense Attorney's kit. Also, [b][i]DO NOT, UNDER NO CIRCUMSTANCE, USE THE "USE TWICE" VARIANT OF THIS MOVE.[/i][/b] The only time you realistically should is if you kill someone with the first hit and want an extra 5 ult bar. Otherwise, 3+3 is inarguably Defense Attorney's worst move in his whole kit. Incredibly unsafe, lackluster reward, wonky hitbox, and very easy to react to, this variant stinks. Even if you land the interruption on the first hit of this variant, a front dash + m1s will always deal more damage. Never use it. Unless you want to style on someone.

[b][i]UNLIKE [/i][/b]its disappointing brother, [i](Judgement's Reach's "Use Twice" variant)[/i] this move is actually a little useful. Sure it's plenty punishable on whiff, but it's also quick enough to be used after No Escape and long enough to net some hits. It's probably not the [i]best[/i] option you have after hitting someone with your No Escape, but with so many options your opponent has to look out for after you land R you can very easily condition them into falling for this move. If you land it, you can also confirm 4 from most ranges off of it, which is always nice. Also, sometimes when you flick this move around with your camera, the hitbox might sometimes lag behind where you [i]think[/i] it should be, leading to some... [i]weird[/i] results.
