Crazy movement tool. Use it to run in or out of situations almost whenever you please. It has practically no endlag, so you can follow up after this move with basically anything you want to supplement an approach. M1s, R, 4, even 2 is a solid answer. Plus, because of the slightly upwards angle it sends at, at certain ranges you can end up right on top of the opponents head, setting up for a crossup with your m1s. You can also kiiinda bait evasive with it? Since it and its non-r-variant counterpart have the same startup, you can sometimes trick people into wasting evasive to avoid the normal move by just using 3+r right in front of a ragdolled opponent. Better opponents might just realize that getting hit by normal 3 doesn't really hurt too bad, though, so sometimes you'll just end up looking a little silly.

This move is [i](outside of some matchups)[/i] exclusively combo food. It's incredibly safe from evasive after 2, alongside being a true ragdoll that combos into 4 and R+4 [i](you can also situationally combo it into 2 if you do Grapple out of an uppercut)[/i], while also setting up for mix with R if those moves are off cooldown. So what about those matchups? matchup-specific interactions Unlike Locust Guy's flight, which only catches airborne targets if they're ragdolled, Grapple catches airborne targets regardless of if they're ragdolled or not. This can lead to some unique and consistent punishes either by using evasive after getting hit by or on reaction to certain moves, all of which will be listed below. [i][b]Honored One:[/b][/i] Air Reversal Red + R [i][b]Vessel:[/b][/i] Air Cursed Strikes, Air Crushing Blow[i] (sometimes)[/i] [i][b]Restless Gambler[/b][/i] Shutter Doors [i](bounce)[/i] [i][b]Blood Manipulator[/b][/i] Air Flowing Red Scale [i](if they use the convergence orb to bounce off of afterwards you can sometimes catch them then as well)[/i] [i][b]Cursed Partners:[/b][/i] Air Rika Launch [i][b]Puppet Master:[/b][/i] Boost On, Puppet Barrage [i][b]Head of the Hei:[/b][/i] Framed Cursory Impact, Decisive Strike [i](if done after Framed Cursory Impact)[/i] [b][i]True Cannon:[/i][/b] Air Second Helping [i](just use it if they use appetizer into Second Helping)[/i] [i][b]Register:[/b][/i] Littering, Speed Crash [i](sometimes)[/i] [i][b]Locust Guy:[/b][/i] any air combo lol [i][b]Star Rage:[/b][/i] Garuda Stab + R [i](keep in mind you might just get cancelled by the huge hitbox anyways)[/i] [i][b]Aspiring Mangaka:[/b][/i] Air Shut Up! [i][b]Crow Charmer:[/b][/i] any air combo lol

4 and all of its variants are all varying degrees of useful for Defense Attorney. All of these variants are great neutral skips and pokes, as they pushback on block and are hard to punish properly. On hit, however, normal 4 cannot true combo into anything. This is where the "mixup-based" part comes into play. After the initial kick, you enter a run where you're free to use 1, 2, or press 4 again to follow up. Remember; none of these options will be true off of the kick, and all of them have their strengths and weaknesses. This is why, normally, when you get the opponent in a combo without their evasive, you'll want to just go for R+4 instead as it's a true combo extend that you don't have to risk missing the mixup on. There's only one case which you shouldn't do this, being after R+3, as typically your r will be on cooldown after landing the slam. But when you know your opponent has evasive, it's a lot easier to sneak this move into untrue combos due to its hard to react to startup when compared to R+4, which requires you to throw your mallet beforehand, essentially telling the opponent what you intend to do. For the normal variant (4 or 4+4), it's a risky combo extender/combo starter, and there's 2 ways that you should use this move. 1: Land the first hit of 4, press 4 again IMMEDIATELY when you get within range to avoid getting the move cancelled/dashed out of. 2: Land the first hit of 4, run straight at the opponent and turn around right as you get slightly behind them to cross up their block. This is risky, but the more you go for 4+4 the more opponents will try to anticipate you going for 4+4, which is when you start using the other variants of this move to punish their block. It's also important to note that another use of this move is to net kills; the execution hp requirement is very lenient (around 15 hp), giving this move a huge window where it's an easy kill in neutral given its speed and overall safety.

Probably the least useful follow up from 4 out of the 3, but it still can do some stuff. First of all, most important thing to know when it comes to this move: unlike 4 + 1, this move can be countered AND you can get hit during the windup. It has the benefit of actually dealing damage on hit as a result, but since you just used up 2 of your ragdoll-hitting moves to use this move you aren't really getting that much off of that hit. You can sometimes sneak in a Grapple if you land this against an opponent who doesn't block it, but typically it's better to go for R after on hit to reset your pressure since 4 + 2 > 3 isn't all that consistent. It's definitely not a bad move. It's probably the most "safe" option to go for after 4, since you can't be punished for guessing wrong with it unless they have a counter. But you're not playing this character because you wanna play safe, are you.

With his many mobility options to approach and engage with the enemy, Defense Attorney is able to keep pressuring Honored One, discouraging them from using any pokes such as Reversal Red or Limitless. A well-timed 1+R can and WILL guardbreak a Limitless! However, Defense Attorney only has 90 HP, and Honored One's heavy hitting combos will ensure that even under pressure, they are still a very present threat throughout the fight. Getting caught by Honored One without evasive will usually spell death for the Defense Attorney... Check out the 81.25 damage combo in Honored One's page. While the Defense Attorney will have an easy time keeping pressure on the Honored One, the Honored One's highly damaging combos are no joke. There's also a little silly thing you can do as Defense Attorney against a lot of characters with unsafe ragdolls [i](e.g. Vessel's Black Flash and Restless Gambler's Fever Breaker) [/i]which is using evasive right after getting hit by the move in question, and IMMEDIATELY using Justice Served. This is, a lot of the time, a free guardbreak, as most of the time these two characters will be holding block either right after using the move or on reaction to evasive in order to avoid getting punished by m1s. And guess what... Honored One has one of these evasive-punishable moves as well, in the form of Rapid Punches! And unlike Vessel and Restless Gambler, Honored One doesn't have a counter, meaning that you can use this to your hearts content... ...is what [i]WOULD [/i] be true if it was 100% consistent. If the Honored One predicts correctly, they're able to dash away from your 2 and get a free punish WHILE you're without your evasive, and if you've read the aforementioned advice you know how well that ends for you. Use this... [i]"technique" [/i]sparingly, but always keep it in mind as it gives incredible reward on a correct prediction. Also keep in mind that though raw Justice Served might not deal that much damage on its own, the psychic damage of getting guardbroken or even just hit by a YOLO raw Justice Served can shake up the mindset of the player you're fighting in a way that constantly makes them question what you're doing next.

Even though Defense Attorney fares much better than most other characters against Blood Manipulator thanks to his outstanding mobility, Supernova unfortunately completely shuts down all of them due to the straightforwardness of his mobility moves. R+R is a straight jump, 3+R is still a straight jump, and 4+Move is much too reactable to rely on. With a cleverly positioned Supernova, the Defense Attorney player is essentially helpless, and your best bet in this situation is to short-hop using R+S+R to bait out the Supernova. Aside from that, all of Blood Manipulator's moves are relatively difficult to punish with short endlags, meaning Defense Attorney's guardbreaking variants will have a much harder time capitalizing on them. Overall, a disadvantageous matchup.

Defense Attorney's 1+R can guardbreak against Switcher's Boogie Woogie. Catching the Switcher in Boogie Woogie's startup OR endlag means a free front dash & M1 chain, without the need to dash up next to the Switcher due to 1+R's deceptively large hitbox. Once the enemy has been hit at least once by your 1+R, the pressure of this variant may deter them from attempting to mixup with Boogie Woogie during the remainder of the match, giving you a way easier time fighting them thanks to Switcher's otherwise lacking neutral.
Mirror matchup! Always act before the enemy, and do not hesitate to use 1+R at any given moment. If your sweep comes out while theirs is still in windup, you will guardbreak them.

Defense Attorney's guardbreaks are a defining aspect of his kit, most of which are immune to counters. Cursed Partners' access to a parry in [i]Outburst[/i] (capable of parrying all of Defense Attorney's guardbreaks), however, somewhat shuts down a lot of Defense Attorney's rushdown and forces you to be a lot more reliant on m1s. It's not a perfect counter to Defense Attorney's rushdown, however; you can mix up the timing (e.g. conditioning after 4 by doing 4+1 or 4+4 quickly in succession, then doing 4 all the way through to catch the parry) and a lot of the time you can still land your guardbreaks on Cursed Partners players once they use [i]Outburst[/i]. Alongside this, Defense Attorney doesn't really have much in the way to reliably and safely deal with and punish Cursed Partners' rushdown. You have to play patient and read your opponent's offensive habits and defensive habits with [i]Outburst[/i] in order to win this matchup.

Since higuruma has multiple (and good) gap closers its hard for a ryu to make distance from a higuruma to safely use his R (especially when in burnout) or zone out a higuruma in general on top of this, higurumas grapple acts as an [b]anti air[/b] one of ryus strongest aspects is his evasive bait making him hard to punish however a higuruma can use his grapple after evasiving from a ryu who used second helping to punish them (since grapple true ragdolls this allows higuruma to combo the ryu) you can either predict the second helping for an anti air punish or eat the damage and evasive afterwards to punish them anyways

After a wing throw, higuruma can evasive and then grapple which acts as an [b]anti air[/b] if the locust does not block, they take 11 damage and are put into true ragdoll which can lead to combo extensions if locust DOES block, grapple deals no damage but still stuns them so you get a combo anyways the locust can avoid this interaction by keeping the higuruma on ground and aiming upwards

Higuruma's sweep is the primary factor in this matchup, as the only moves in Charles' kit that don't outright lose to it are Clairvoyance and aerial Shut Up. As such, you can engage a lot more comfortably than most characters, as he has to actually respect your mix. No Escape can be countered with Eye Catching, but you can easily call this out by recalling your gavel early or missing on purpose.

Since Crow Charmer also has air combos [i](are you seeing a pattern here)[/i] grapple acts as an anti air here aswell but you need to be much faster and in some cases you'll need to predict it, since so much of her kit air combos we wont list every interaction here just know that if she's in the air you can evasive and catch her with grapple to start your own combo Aside from combos, if she just uses R to go in the air or uses Bird control to fly in the air you can use grapple there as well. However, Defense Attorney has no real safe answer to her oppressive options (divine bird control and murmurate) plus she has the option to ground combo you so this is not an advantageuous matchup

Disaster Plants is a set play zoner who controls the battlefield and plays from range punishing reckless approaches. While threatening devastating combos with ranged blockbreakers from afar. This however comes at a cost as Disaster Plants possess single M1s rather than a string of short-ranged melee jabs, with her uppercuts gaining increased range at the cost of being unable to interrupt actions, thus she is extremely vulnerable in M1 trades.

Disaster Plants ideally wants to stay just out of the enemy's reach (around side dash range). After that the rest of Disaster Plants gameplan varies based on the actions of the opponent. Disaster plants should avoid ANY M1 TRADING as her entire gameplan revolves entirely around almost completely forgoing it unless utterly necessary - and her kit does very well to facilitate it. If the opponent is aggressive/approaching, Disaster Plants should focus on keeping distance away from melee range and weaving around enemy attacks, to find openings to punish periods where the enemy is vulnerable, stuck in the middle of a skill's startup or recovery. Disaster Plants should ideally aim to turn their aggression into an opportunity to combo start, punishing excessively bold approaches with their own moves. If the opponent is passive, Disaster Plants should attempt to break the stand-off using an unexpected Root Swarm or Defense Response while remaining at mid-range to avoid getting punished. A passive opponent should be pressured to never stay still for long at threat of a surprise Root Swarm, while agile opponents who focus on dodging can still be hit by a well-Aimed Aerial Defense Response due to the fact it can be steered during its use. Disaster Plants must be careful to not leave themselves vulnerable while still keeping up controlled aggression and pressure on her passive opponents. In terms of managing evasive, it is critical that the Disaster Plants remains very aware of their opponent's evasive meter and tries to gauge it throughout the fight - this is because a majority of Disaster Plants' moves are very evasive punishable if not used safely - Lasso shouldn't be used to combo start as it reels the opponent right into close-range for them to easily punish the Disaster Plants after a downslam or uppercut with their own m1s after an evasive. Root Swarm should only be used at a medium-long range in order to spawn a Spike and after evasive is used elsewise it will result in an evasive punish as it knocks opponents towards the Disaster Plants, also allowing an easy evasive punish into m1s. It is also risky to use Aerial Defense Response too close as it can be interrupted on its startup - and is telegraphed by a jump, so Disaster Plants should try to hit it farther away. Additionally, if Disaster Plants misses/whiffs one of her moves at this range, it could be devastating, nearly always resulting in any competent opponent landing a combo due to harsh endlag locking them in place. Disaster Plants' kit is geared towards giving the opponent alot of evasive meter due to the extremely punishing high-damage nature of their combos - so they should always be conscious of creating distance towards the end of a combo for fear of being evasive punished. Rarely will an opponent be purely passive or purely aggressive. A good Disaster Plants should be able to read and adapt to their opponent as the fight changes states.

Positioning is key to Disaster Plants as her moves vary in effectiveness at different ranges - often having poorer value or safety at closer range, and bolstering more benefits at a long range - where the drawback is needing, often, to bait a sidedash out. Luckily, Disaster Plants' moveset excels in baiting out sidedash - with multiple moves geared towards it, such as Aerial/Grounded Defense Response, Plant Guidance Surging Thorns (though Plant Guidance does require precise aim) - which then allow her to punish with the other remaining moves in her kit. What makes Disaster Plants notoriously strong is the fact that when compared to all of the other characters in the game, she operates on an entirely unique set of fundamentals - completely disregarding the standard everybody else works by. As opposed to focusing on engaging with m1s, dashes and approaching by using skills that compliment their kit's capability to approach, Hanami instead focuses not on trading m1s with her opponent but almost entirely on applying the latent potential her moves have in neutral and trying to land these moves by focusing on good spacing and making distance - Root Swarm with its long-range, unblockable hitbox, Air Defense Response with its unblockable hitbox, and less-punishable endlag - essentially, she should threaten a sidedash using a multitude of her tools before punishing it at a range with the aforementioned optimal combo starters. She has approximately FIVE different ways to start a combo, so despite lacking evasive bait, she can still be a big enough threat to choke an evasive out. [b]Close Range / Melee Range[/b] Extremely vulnerable, leaving the Disaster Plants prone to m1s or grab skills. At this range, Disaster Plants has few reliable options to make distance or relieve pressure - however, they are not fully out of luck. - The Disaster Plants can mark the ground right below them for Plant Guidance, then block a sidedash m1 and use Plant Guidance Surging Thorns, knocking the opponent up into the air. This can also be done preemptively, but is riskier as it is more on prediction that way. - The same thing can be done with Plant Guidance Defense Response, spawning a small flower field applying daze on use of any offensive moves - do note that the daze only works once, as if the opponent uses an attack again they wont be afflicted with the affect any more times. The lesser damage and counter-based gimmick makes it obsolete next to its Surging Thorns Plant Guidance counterpart despite the marginally larger aoe, which can deal additional damage and true stun with its potential to guardbreak on block and interrupt in a fashion similar to Salaryman. - Old reliable (block and) sidedash neutral m1 - because Disaster Plants' neutral m1 has true stun, she can create distance by retaliating with her own neutral m1 and backdashing away safely - as it cannot be evasived out of. - Additionally, she could Iframe through a melee move and knockback using Grounded Defense Response - though she should be careful not to be interrupted on its startup - As a last ditch effort, she could use a risky close range Root Swarm to knock an opponent away [b]Mid Range / Sidedash Range[/b] Disaster Plants is far less vulnerable (though not totally out of the woods in terms of being punishable..get it), with the benefit of having access to maximize value from her offensive tools due to the space letting her go without instantly being interrupted. This is a good distance to lay down pressure and be aggressive, enabling Disaster Plants to really, thoroughly continue keeping space and controlling the pace of the fight. [b]Surging Thorns[/b] isn't too optimal in neutral, being a blockable poke with a nicher user as a mix option, like on getup if block isn't held to build a habit punishable with a guardbreak from Surging Thorns Plant Guidance. On the brightside, it pushes back on hit AND block, and has short enough recovery for the Hanami to turn and block an m1 evasive punish on hit or sidedash m1 punish if used on block. Should only REALLY be used if the user is sure to land it. [u]Usually not recommended[/u] as it serves a greater purpose as an extension tool to stall for cooldowns. [b]Root Swarm and Aerial/Grounded Defense Response [/b]both share a function as ranged blockbreakers - [u]these 2 moves should be used in tandem with eachother[/u], in where the Hanami uses one of them at a safe range to threaten a hit or combo and waste sidedash/evasive, [u]before punishing with the other remaining move[/u]. Disaster Plants should be weary that both of these moves are [b]telegraphed[/b] and have noticeable startup - Root Swarm with its[b] reactable [/b]startup, and Air Defense Response with the initial jump to use it telegraphing its use. Additionally, they both have harsher endlag, leaving them vulnerable to a potential evasive punishh - so she should try to bait evasive beforehand by using safe combo routes and building damage to pressure the use of it. [b]Flower Field (Plant Guidance Defense Response)[/b] as interruption/counter that can be used to combo start..though is [b]made redundant[/b] by: [b]Plant Guidance Surging Thorns[/b] a blockbreaking extension and combo-starting tool which has guardbreaking properties similar to Salaryman - proc'ing guardbreak on skill interruption or block. While harder to hit than the other combo starters, if it guardbreaks it is uniquely the safest combo starting tool as it has true stun, disabling evasive as an option for her opponent and making it totally unpunishable - allowing a safe conversion with a move like backdash Root Swarm. - This move also makes Plant Guidance Root Swarm redundant too - as while the Root Swarm Plant Guidance gives less evasive, its marginal, and at the caveat of dealing 4 instead of 9/12 damage (less than half!) and only working on ragdoll - while Plant Guidance Surging Thorns does 9/12, hits ragdoll, standing, AND can guardbreak for more damage and true stun. [u]Plant Guidance Surging Thorns is KING and the go-to of the Plant Guidance moves for not only combo starting safely in neutral without dashbait but also combo extending safely. Basically prioritize using this over its counterparts, which it feature-creeps in every way.[/u] [b]Uppercut[/b] is a low risk option thanks to its properties of having an extended range and auto-tracking any opponent in that range. Can be used to combo start or lock down opponents for a short time, stun will still apply even if it does not interrupt actions, can be used to slowdown approaches or convert into other moves. Also the best combo extension tool in the kit, allowing her to string it between multiple moves by hitting ragdoll with an uppercut on little to no cooldown, unlike any other final m1, making Hanami as good as she is at stalling for cooldowns in a combo. [b]Budshot[/b] can be used to interrupt opponents in a pinch, [u]not recommended [/u] - only really usable for interrupting high startup moves at a range, like Yuki's Mass Breaker or Nanami's Blunt Cut. [b]Long Range / Beyond Frontdash Range[/b] Comfortable, it's[b] the best spot for a Disaster Plants to avoid punishment while still being capable of offensive pressure and punishment herself.[/b] This is the ideal range to capitalize on whiff punishing her opponent with her long-range blockbreakers. [b]Aerial Defense Response[/b] and [b]RootSwarm[/b] serve their initial functions, albeit even harder to punish thanks to the additional distance alleviating the harsh endlag. [b]Budshot[/b] as poke projectile, serving its initial function again [b]Lasso[/b] (Hanami's unique long-range frontdash that keeps her immobile and instead reaches to grab the opponent) can be used as a slower blockable rootswarm thanks to its high range, though compared to it, it's more lackluster due to being blockable. Can still be greating at grabbing opponents locked in high endlag from a move on whiff, like Yuki's Mass Breaker or Yuji's Cursed Strikes. [u]Not recommended [/u] otherwise, though, as trying to use it freely in neutral can result in a free punish due to its high endlag and blockable nature. [b]Very Long Range / Twice the Range of Frontdash or more[/b] The[b] safest position[/b] - out of range from most threatening attacks, any attacks that may hit are much easier for the Disaster Plants to avoid..though the same goes for their opponent, making her own attacks particularly difficult to hit in how telegraphed they are. if a Disaster Plants must disengage, it is ideal to remain at long range. Her only real attacking options are below..not that she should be in this range since they're made virtually useless and easy to avoid. She should simply try stay just out of ONE frontdash's range instead. [b]Lasso (frontdash)[/b] keeps the same functionalty [b]Root Swarm[/b] keeps the same functionality [u]NEITHER recommended, extremely telegraphed from so far away. She should not stray too far and stay at the range of one frontdash instead of two to maximize her offense and defense. [/u]

Disaster Plants lacks a definitive evasive bait option, instead aim for safe non committal combo routes [i](usually by creating distance/back dashing before using a move) [/i] [u]until the opponent naturally uses up evasive due to the cumulative damage[/u]. These can be found in the combos tab. Traditional Evasive punishing with Disaster Plants M1s - due to the heavy endlag of Neutral M1 allowing Disaster Plants - instead leaves herself to be punished if she whiffs. [u]Surging Thorns[/u] or [u]Aerial Defense Response[/u] can be used in it's place, [u]Plant Guidance Surging Thorns[/u] can be used in order to punish and proc true stun guardbreak to convert if the opponent is still in endlag or startup after evasive. While positioning is much more lenient then an M1 evasive punish these options being slower then an M1 means Disaster Plants requires a longer punish window then regular characters in order to reliably evasive punish.

[b]The player shoots two spikes forwards in rapid succession, and then follows up with a wall of spikes.[/b] The effective range of this move is around 5x melee range. Surging Thorns is a relatively simple move compared to others in Disaster Plant's kit, and comes with only two uses. It can be used as both combo filler and a mixup option in neutral. Surging Thorns' ability to hit ragdolled and grounded ragdolled opponents makes it easy to incorporate into any combo, and can continue red after all three types of M1. The large effective range of this move can also help start a combo in neutral, as it can hit outside of regular M1 range, leading to less punishment. Surging Thorns also comes out very quickly, which can help with this. This move comes with large endlag on block and can be evaded at the end, making it very risky to use on opponents with full evasive bar. A simple way to prevent punishment on use is to use your Plant Guidance ability in the middle of this move. Using Flower Field or Root Spike can help keep you safe if the opponent tries to evasive.

[b]The player shoots two buds from their hands in rapid succession.[/b] Effective range of the projectiles is 70 studs. The buds push players within 35 studs, and pull those at longer range. When a bud collides with a player, it expands and flowers on their chest. These budded flowers can stack multiple times, and last for an infinite amount of time. When a target connected to budded flowers uses a move, the flowers are sacrificed to remove 7 seconds of the Disaster Plant's special (Plant Guidance). This allows the player to use their special in rapid succession, leading to safer combos, more combo tools, and extra block-breaking moves. Bud Shot is also great for stacking many roots with Plant Guidance, and can help set up more consistent traps. Bud Shot is a vital tool for any Disaster Plants user, and is regularly seen as unappreciated and useless (which is false). There are [u][b]four ways[/b][/u] to use Bud Shot effectively in a fight: [b]1. Use at the start of an encounter, when given an unpunishable opening.[/b] The best way to do this is to hit your regular M1, which cannot be evaded and lets you easily lead into your buds. Another effective way to hit your buds is using them after your opponent is in the end lag of a move. Using your buds at the start of the fight lets you use your special twice in rapid succession, which can easily catch your opponent off-guard if they try to punish with an evasive. [b]2. Use at the end of a combo.[/b] Since Bud Shot isn't an effective combo tool, using it at the end of a combo is the most effective. If you already had used your special during the combo, it lets you reduce the cooldown quickly, which can help with punishing the opponent if they try to pressure you with their evasive. [b]3. Use to knock ragdolled opponents into roots.[/b] Since Bud Shot can hit ragdolled players, if someone is ragdolled but doesn't quite reach your roots to extend a combo, budshot can be used to push the player into your roots. This rarely ever happens, however can be a vital tool if the time comes. [b]4. Use when in neutral.[/b] Bud Shot can be blocked, which can lead to being punished. However, using Bud Shot in neutral can do the same job as [b]1.[/b] (Just less effective). Only use this option as a last resort if you cannot put the enemy into a combo (such as fighting a Lucky Coward that cancels your moves). The extra Plant Guidance can help you push back pressure and regain an upperhand in the fight.

Hanami's combo game is exceptionally linear - [b]she should prioritize using safe combos[/b] that wont get her punished to accumulate damage on an opponent, eventually accumulating enough damage to choke out an evasive to avoid damage or until the opponent is impatient enough to try and punish. [u][b]Afterwards,[/u] she can reach full damage output and execute a full length combo.[/b] However, as with any other character, she should always track the opponent's evasive bar during combos and be familiar with their evasive gain - this is exceptionally important for a character like Disaster Plants as she utilises combos which, in exchange for being so highly-damaging and effective in stalling for cooldowns due to their length, [b]refund almost all of the opponent's evasive after a full length combo[/b]. [u]She should try position safer towards the end of a combo, generally.[/u] Additionally, Hanami[b] should be trying extra hard to stall [/b]out for her cooldowns. She should be using the lengthiness of her combos in order to stall out for cooldowns and get moves back near the end of the combo, proving very helpful for when she returns to neutral afterwards and need options back - so it's very noteworthy.

Against Honored One, Disaster Plants' gameplan of keeping away and using moves becomes significantly worse, due to Honored One's [b]special being able to teleport behind[/b] Disaster Plants, which can also punish moves such as [b]Root Swarm[/b] and [b]Aerial Defense Response[/b], due to their noticable endlag when missed. Plant Guidance's Block-Breaking Spike or Flower Field may be able to circumvent this by hitting/interrupting Honored One as they teleport, but this requires planning ahead since the teleport's windup is significantly faster than both options, making it a situational counter. In close range, it comes down to if Disaster Plants can land [b]Defense Response[/b] or if Honored One can bypass Disaster Plants' block either by[b] side-dashing or using Rapid Punches[/b]. Using[b] Plant Guidance's Flower Field[/b] here is significantly better as you retreat since Honored One doesn't have a way to reliably hit a defensive Disaster Plants with ranged options. To summarise this, Honored One can take advantage of Disaster Plants' long endlag for whiffing while Disaster Plants has few options to defend themselves from that. When facing Honored One, Disaster Plants must ensure that they don't recklessly spam moves from afar, while keeping track of Honored One's teleport.

Against Vessel, Disaster Plants has to worry about the sheer mobility Vessel has, with Aerial Crushing Blow being able to avoid attacks such as Root Swarm and Lasso, while Aerial Cursed Strikes is able to avoid Aerial Defense Response (with a stricter timing). Due to Vessel's aggressive nature, Disaster Plants needs to ensure that they are able to keep pace with them, and respond accordingly. In this matchup, both sides have their own advantages. Vessel can easily approach and dodge the attacks of Disaster Plants. Plant Guidance's Flower Field, which would usually be useful in handling aggressive opponents can be bypassed by Vessel using Aerial Cursed Strikes and Crushing Blow to engage, with the former being unblockable as well. If a Disaster Plants gets desperate and uses Defense Response recklessly, Vessel can use Manji Kick to counter them, effectively wasting Disaster Plants' main keep-away tool. Disaster Plants isn't all hopeless against all this however, Vessel's kit lacks neutral options other than their feinting and M1s, giving Disaster Plants ways to keep away and defend themselves in case a Vessel approaches, like using Root Swarm up close to catch Vessel off-guard, or using Defense Response as a Vessel blocks, which can also lead into a combos. Disaster Plants also has a huge advantage at range (obviously), if a Vessel were to avoid Disaster Plants' attacks from afar, they'd need to react fast enough to either block or dodge certain attacks, if they react wrongly (e.g blocking during Aerial Defense Response, getting caught by Surging Thorns' relatively quick windup), they can easily be placed into combos by Disaster Plants. Plant Guidance can assist in placing Flower Field in case Disaster Plants whiffs an attack, and since Vessel primarily relies on getting close, the usual side-dash M1 would get cancelled, or the Vessel has to reposition to find another opportunity. In short, while Vessel has ways to get up close, it is under the assumption that they are able to react to every single attack that Disaster Plants can dish out, while Disaster Plants does have more options to defend themselves in case the Vessel gets close.

With Restless Gambler having few options of initiating outside of side-dash M1s, this matchup favours Disaster Plants with their ability to keep away and attack from mid-range. Restless Gambler draws the short stick in an usual engagement, they lack ways to reliably close the distance between Disaster Plants and themselves. Unlike other M1 Merchants such as Vessel and Head of the Hei, who actually have reliable ways to close the gap, Restless Gambler's only option is... [b]Shutter Doors + Reserve Balls[/b] which can be used to threaten a combo after Disaster Plants whiffs [b]Root Swarm or Aerial Defense Response[/b]. If Restless Gambler gets close, it can be cut short with a [b]Plant Guidance's Flower Patch or Thorn Impale[/b], Disaster Plants has little to worry about in terms of engaging a Restless Gambler, even an interaction as insignificant as Restless Gambler using Door Guard which can't fully defend against something like [b]Bud Shot[/b] (since the 2nd bud hits). with obvious caution to evasive punishes and close range encounters especially since Door Guard still functions as a counter, which can punish moves such as Defense Response

Generic "C tier" M1 merchant with all the standard tools needed to win at JJS. Safe poke options, fast block breakers, rushdown tools, strong evasive baits, and big combo damage. While Honored One doesn't majorly excel in any category, he also doesn't lack whats necessary.

Limitless's startup and low endlag make it quite viable as a neutral tool. Lapse Blue and Twofold Kick leave you open for quite a while on block/miss. Reversal Red may look like a decent poke tool but won't lead into much on its own. Rapid Punches can be used to cheese some M1 trades.

Lapse Blue is your most consistent combo tool due to its Low CD, and safe conversion into limitless. Due to limitless applying true rag-doll, the threat of conversion forces the opponent to evasive to avoid a 47.75 DMG combo. Strengths: Completely safe depending on the matchup, MAJORLY threatening, and decent stall. Weaknesses: Since Limitless -> Rapid punches is green, in match ups involving a counter this combo path is no longer a guaranteed evasive bait. Mind games and such. M1 M1 M1 Lapse Blue Limitless Rapid Punches Strengths: Completely safe, highly threatening, and saves a valuable CD (rapid punches). Weaknesses: Less damage, less stall, and less opportunities to bait evasive after the combo if your opponent chooses to hold evasive. M1 M1 M1 LAPSE BLUE LIMITLESS REVERSAL RED

Since everything leads into itself, there isn't much difficulty converting off of a lucky hit and such. Do note that Twofold Kick allows you to sneak an M1 during the enemy's fall, and that Rapid Punches could be lead into an uppercut on wakeup. Here's a combo whenever the stars align for you: M1 M1 M1 Uppercut Rapid Punches Twofold Kick Jump M1 M1 Reversal Red M1 Downslam Lapse Blue Limitless Ragdoll cancel should be regained right after Lapse Blue, but there's no harm in adding an Aerial Kick for good measure.

A highly punishable, ranged grab-and-pull move. While weak in neutral play, it serves as a reliable combo tool in the Honored One's kit. Targeting an enemy within 35 studs with crosshair allows Honored One to pull them in, dealing 5 damage. Upon pulling the target, Honored One gains temporary melee I-frames and kicks the enemy high into the air for an additional 7.5 damage (12.5 total damage).

A solid neutral tool that is normally blockable, but can be set up to bypass blocks entirely—making it the second-best neutral option in Honored One's kit. Shoots a slow, blockable projectile that explodes on impact or automatically detonates after traveling 40 studs (with a 15-stud AoE). Deals 12.5 damage on hit and 6.25 chip damage on block.

A fast point-blank teleport move that lets Honored One bypass an opponent's block and punish defensive playstyles, making it a great mix-up option against defending enemies. Aiming the special variant at an airborne target causes Honored One to kick them into a direct Red, dealing 17.5 total damage (5 for the kick, 12.5 for Red). While this attack is blockable and interruptible during its initial setup, it bypasses ragdoll to override the kick’s knockback for optimal combo path extensions.

A fast airborne move that lets Honored One instantly punish airborne opponents, making it a strong option against vertical strategies. When aiming the special variant at an airborne target, Honored One executes a kick and immediately follows it with a direct Reversal Red, delivering a combined 17.5 damage (5 for the kick, 12.5 for Red). While this attack is blockable and interruptible during its setup, it bypasses ragdoll to override the kick’s default knockback, keeping the enemy accessible, though executing it will put all used abilities on cooldown.

A fast counter move that lets Honored One instantly punish aggressive opponents and stop their ongoing attacks completely, making it a strong option against hasty strategies. Interrupting an enemy's action with the previous variant stuns them in place before Honored One releases Red, dealing 15 damage on hit. A great neutral option that often punishes aggressive playstyles and uncareful use of moves, forcing opponents to think twice before committing to reckless attacks.

A strong combo tool that bypasses blocks by grabbing Honored One's enemies, delivering a high-damage flurry of strikes before knocking targets far away—making it an effective guard-break option against defensive opponents. Honored One initiates a spinning kick to grab a nearby enemy, unleashing a barrage of strikes that ends with a final blow dealing 17.25 total damage and launching the target into a ragdoll state. While this attack is unblockable and grants melee and bullet i-frames during the punch barrage, it is interruptible during startup and cannot bypass ragdoll, being on a 15-second cooldown.

A neat combo tool that pops enemies into the air for big air follow-ups and high-damage combo routes, though its long recovery makes it easily punishable on miss. Honored One swings an upward kick that freezes the target in place before following up with an unblockable second strike, dealing 10 total damage (6 for the first kick, 4 for the second) and launching them sky-high. While this attack bypasses ragdoll and grants melee i-frames on hit, it is semi-blockable and interruptible, operating on an 18-second cooldown.

Honored One consists of a fairly complete kit, one that has very intentional design from the developers; making him simpler and less complicated in terms of tech. However, there are some niche capabilities that can truly spice up gameplay, especially in regards to his already beast level combo damage, as well as adding a little more neutral to compensate for his M1 trading status.

This is a very basic application of limitless. Limitless Turn Around 180° Side Dash (Optional) Essentially this is probably the most popular and easy to use neutral tech of Honored One, and for good reason; it always catches players, incuding high level ones off guard.

If someone catches Honored One's limitless turn around, there is a good way to decieve them and to trick their direction. Limitless Turn Around 360° Side Dash (optional) Editor's Note: I've only seen this used at a high level.
One of Honored One's most popular combo tech. Lapse Blue / Twofold Kick Limitless (Air SLam) Turn Around 180° (before slam) Side Dash M1 / Rapid Punches OR Front Dash

Image description The HUD is an integral part of any game, especially fighting games. and JJS is no exception to this rule. the HUD's utility ranges from convenient at best to borderline detrimental when absent. this includes the player HP, hotbar, character select, emote purchasing, settings and even the transfer from other gamemodes

Image description The health bar (usually shown on the top right of your screen) shows your HP. however, the health bar shows your HP by precent compared to your character's health. a 100 HP character would reach half HP on 50%. however characters like vesel, ten shadows and puppet master reach 50% at around 42.5%

Image description In JJS, you can build an "awakening" meter by dealing damage. around 285 points of damage points are required for a full ultimate meter to fill up. some characters (puppet master, sky assassin, perfection's awakening) do have a rainbow meter at the lower part of their awakening one that determines their special ultimate property. Below the awakening bar lie the special and evasive bars. the special bar displays the cooldown of the respective character's special. it goes on a set cooldown dependent on each character's special. The evasive meter, unlike your special, fills up gradually with the amount of damage you take and deal. but taking damage usually fills it up more than dealing it, around 76.9 damage points need to be taken for a full evasive meter to fill up. or 200 damage deals. however, when below 50HP, your evasive meter gains a noticeable boost of speed. reaching a full evasive meter in an astounding 62.5 damage taken and around 100 damage dealt. keep in mind that this boost takes effect when reaching 50 HP flat. so characters with lower HP pools (lucky coward, sky assassin) reach this threshold faster than a 100 HP character would. thus giving them an advantage when it comes to the mechanic of evasive

Locust Guy, the antithesis of a balanced design, is the simplest M1 Merchant that JJS has to offer in terms of everything: combo game, neutral engagement, strategy, techs, and more. Thus, Locust Guy is one of the easiest character to learn and to play effectively, even at major level. He is defined by his insanely powerful evasive baits and air combos. In fact, Locust Guy completely nullifies the Evasive mechanic of the game whenever he is in a fight, making him the ultimate fundamentals check. This strength is further enhanced by his complete safety when it comes to engaging with Sidedash M1 and combos. All of his M1s are completely safe on Block, his combos are unpunishable, and his damage is high. In exchange, Locust Guy sacrifices every single possible neutral application of his skills, leaving only behind Sidedash M1 and a 16s short air dash. He has high recovery period on every skills, melee skills that are all blockable, and a projectile that doesn't convert into anything when landed.

Locust Guy's skills are not effective at all when throwed out in Neutral: [url=#sec-clever][i]Clever[/i][/url] is blockable and has great amount of block endlag, [url=#sec-black-mucus][i]Black Mucus[/i][/url] on hit in Neutral can not convert to any options in Locust Guy's kit, [url=#sec-crushing-jaws][i]Crushing Jaws[/i][/url]'s first hit is blockable and slows down the skill immensely if missed; [url=#sec-wing-throw][i]Wing Throw[/i][/url] is blockable, has high block endlag, and has short range; and [url=#sec-fluttering-pounce][i]Fluttering Pounce[/i][/url] is a decent, silent, and quick air dash that is on a 16s cooldown (shared with [color=hsl(100, 100%, 75%)]his [url=#sec-fluttering-pounce-air-combo]Air Combo[/url][/color]) So the only way to play Locust Guy effectively is to rely entirely on the player's fundamentals and mechanical skills such as M1 trading, tracking, blocking, etc. to start a combo. But that's about it, thanks to his air combo game being some of the best evasive bait in the game and also being unpunishable, Locust Guy don't have to worry about the [i]Evasive[/i] aspect of the game and can just keep focusing on winning as many M1 trades as possible. In a way, Locust Guy makes the most out of mastering fundamentals and acts as the fundamentals check for other characters.

Brutal (by: Deptr) Image description Locust Guy's combos are some of the highest damaging and consistent ones to do in the game. Thanks to his incredible evasive bait and safe M1s, Locust Guy's gameplan is to try to do these combos over and over and over again until the opponent dies. There isn't much more to talk about regarding his general gameplan. About [b]baiting evasive[/b], Locust Guy just have to hit either [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] or [i]Wing Throw[/i], and it will guarantee that the opponent evasive instantly 99% of the time. This is majorly due to his air combos gimmick, which can only be avoided if the opponent evasives, otherwise they will be put in an unescapable combo with no counterplay. [url=#sec-read-first]See more here[/url]

This is Locust Guy only semblance of [i]Neutral[/i] beside Sidedash M1, and it is very lackluster. [url=#sec-fluttering-pounce][i]Fluttering Pounce[/i][/url], when used in Neutral, is a 360-directional air dash. The dash itself is very quiet and has a very inconspicuous animation, so it can be used as a jumpscare option to start a combo at sidedash distance, or a second dash similar to Head of the Hei's double dashes. Neutral Fluttering Pounce in action But there is one thing to note about. [url=#sec-fluttering-pounce-air-combo][i]Air Combo[/i][/url] puts the R slot on a 16s cooldown everytime it is used. So if a Locust Guy perform an air combo, there is a real chance that he will rarely ever used the neutral version of this special throughout the match. The best way to make the most use out of this is to stall and play passive, waiting for the 16s cooldown to pass. Here's some of the methods: [b]Neutral Black Mucus[/b]: if landed, Locust Guy creates some distance. If missed, the opponent probably wasted their sidedash to dodge it, limiting their ability to approach and M1 trade. [b]Zoning[/b]: Locust Guy preferably wants to stay just about the max sidedash distance away from the opponent if his current goal is to stall for cooldown or to bait their opponent sidedash. [b]Running Away[/b]: The most effective method of stalling for cooldown as a Locust Guy.

This section covers everything there is to Locust Guy when it comes to "mixups" and "Green Combos". Going for these strategies is an unoptimal way to play Locust Guy, but it can be a lot more fun than playing optimally as a Locust Guy [u][i](The bar is in hell)[/i][/u]. Of course, a successful and lucky usage of these strategies can sometimes make Locust Guy an even stronger character than he is when played optimally; they really depend on the levels of play honestly. [b][i]Keep in mind that, these strategies are untrue, so they are very vulnerable to blocking and counters.[/i][/b]

Thanks to Locust Guy's M1s all having a block endlag of 11f [i](not counting the last M1s)[/i], he can safely M1 his opponent on wake up, block and then M1 again to force an M1 trade for free. This is infamously known as [multicolor=#a3e635,#15803d]The awesome Okizeme Technique[/multicolor]. While being completely green and escapable with a Sidedash, Locust Guy can get more M1s in on the opponent for basically zero risk so long as the technique is properly being performed and he can react to the opponent's actions appropiately. Locust Guy can also get a combo from succesfully winning the M1 trade, which is majorly great. When doing this technique, it is important to have sidedash off cooldown, else the opponent can mix the Locust Guy back with their own sidedash and reverse the situation.

The most popular form of [multicolor=#CB8E00,#00A86B]the Clever Mixups[/multicolor] is to throw out the appropiately named move "[url=#sec-clever]Clever[/url]" in Neutral. The Clever Mixup is best used when the opponent least expects it. As a certain Locust Guy main said: "Clever's lack of a [b]discernible audio cue[/b], combined with its [b]subtle [noauto]startup[/noauto] animation[/b], makes it surprisingly [b][u]difficult to react[/u][/b] to." Crushing Jaws in Neutral is even worse than Clever. It has less hitboxes, is extremely slow, and very reactable. Still, its only redeeming quality is the fact that [i]Crushing Jaws[/i]' second hit is unblockable. So there is a chance that against an opponent who lacks some form of intelligence, it can land in Neutral and net Locust Guy a combo for free. The more practical usage is to use this skill on wakeup. There's 2 ways to do it: [b]Time and Land the first hit[/b]: On success, this would let [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] deal its full damage and continue Locust Guy's Combo. However, it is very precise and very unforgiving. Notes: Black Mucus's ragdoll time can set up a pretty favorable scenario where Locust Guy can perform this consistently, but it is still, again, very precise and unforgiving. [b]Miss the first hit and Land the second hit[/b]: This version is a lot less strict and precise thanks to the second hit being unblockable. But Locust Guy would lose out 4 damage from doing this. Having no effective Neutral abilities, Locust Guy is bound to be hard countered by any character with superior Neutral game. But it isn't as hopeless as it seems (it is still pretty hopeless regardless). Locust Guy still has some tricks to get around some of the most oppresive neutral in the game, and it has to do with [url=#sec-fluttering-pounce]Fluttering Pounce[/url]. [b]"Fly over it"[/b] is a popular way to use the R special. Basically, Locust Guy can fly over quite a few things in this game such as Blood Manipulator's Supernova, Puppet Master's Heat Emission, Disaster Plants' Root Swarm, and more. After avoiding the attack, Locust Guy can come down and roll into the opponent, instantly initiating an M1 trade. [b]Fluttering Jumpscare[/b] is another way that Locust Guy can employ to deal with other characters' Neutral game. The idea is to fly straight into the opponent when they are thinking about how to approach the Locust Guy with their Neutral options. Nine times out of ten, if done correctly, Locust Guy can often catch these opponent by surprise, stopping the opponent's offense and starting a combo. [b]Black Mucus[/b] is a blockbreaking projectile with a decent hitbox size. It ragdolls on hit, which means it can threaten things like Ten Shadows' Divine Dog or Black Death's Earthen Insect Trance. Mentioned earlier, the opponent could choose to burn their sidedash to dodge this attack, which means that Locust Guy now have an advantage to dash in with his own Sidedash M1 and win the engagement. It functions like a microscopic version of Aspiring Mangaka's Clairvoyance, which is to disable the opponent sidedash, giving the attacker the upper hand in engaging and winning that engagement. Usage Notes Video Locust Guy flies over a Supernova orb, dodging its explosion, and catches Blood Manipulator in a combo on the way down [i]Usually it is better to just block instead of flying over it, because reserving Fluttering Pounce to approach is more valuable[/i] [i]Black Mucus[/i] catches a Ten Shadows summoning his dog and disables it [i]This can only realistically be done on prediction. And even then, this won't work on a smart Ten Shadows[/i] Locust Guy flies straight to Disaster Plants, avoiding Aerial Defense Response, and punish her for missing it [i]This is actually a feasible and consistent strategy that Locust Guy can pull off against Disaster Plants[/i] More (Recording vids) Notes this and that

Upon using [i]Clever[/i], Locust Guy throws out a barrage of punches using two of his arms (not four). This attack has multiple continous hitbox, around 14 of them in total; They would together deal 14.2 damage. This skill has a fairly decent startup of 24f with a pretty quick and semi-unpunishable recovery of 15f. However, this skill has a great amount of block endlag of 43f, so it is not recommended to use this skill in Neutral as it can be easily blocked. On hit, Locust Guy gain a +28f advantage over the standing stunned opponent; this advantage can chain to pretty much anything in Locust Guy kit beside [i]Black Mucus[/i].

[i]Clever[/i] is mainly used as a combo extender used in between M1 chains to deal extra damage, however as it does not lead into a full M1 reset like Shut Up! (Aspiring Mangaka), or even an M1 Rewind like Shutter Door or Focus Strike (Restless Gambler and Perfection), but continues where Locust Guy left off. This is due to its M1 remembrance mechanic, where it remembers your last M1 for around a second. This mechanic is also why doing 4 M1s into Clever often leaves Locust Guy unable to M1 for a longer time than usual. Despite being unable to hit ragdoll, Clever can hit aerial ragdoll, meaning if Locust Guy knows his opponent doesn't have evasive, he can get extra damage by using uppercut into Clever, however after Clever Locust Guy are unable to M1 until his opponent is actionable, leaving his only viable moves as [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] and [i]Wing Throw[/i]. There exists a Tech for [i]Clever[/i] that can be considered the kind of viable: Clever can lead to an extra M1 if Clever is used after the first (and only the first) M1, which is called [url=#sec-m1s-farm]Clever Extra M1[/url] There is also another notable Tech that ends an air combo with a [i]Clever[/i]: [url=#sec-m1s-farm]Clever Slam[/url]; this is a great tech as it lets Locust Guy get in an extra Downslam during his combo, or lead into another evasive bait combo thanks to Clever restanding the opponent. Basically, [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] and [i]Wing Throw[/i] are both an option after [i]Clever[/i], instead of just [i]Wing Throw[/i] after a Downslam from an air combo

Wing Throw is Locust Guy's BEST combo extender, due to it's shorter cooldown, ability to hit on ragdoll, and potential to waste opponent evasive if they use it too early, leading to a full combo. Yet Wing Throw much like Crushing Jaws, should not be used in neutral due to its high, reactable startup, on top of being fully blockable. To utilise Wing Throw effectively and set up for Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant (R special), you must aim your camera up after grabbing your opponent so that they are thrown higher in order to extend their ragdoll time. However the most useful thing you can do with Wing Throw (that requires a bit of timing) is throwing your opponent directly upwards and as they are falling catch them with an M1, this leads into a full M1 reset and a combo and is fully red, an alternative to this that is easier is Catching them with Clever due to its larger hitbox that lasts longer, which also leads into an M1 reset and combo.

Fluttering Pounce is Locust Guy's only mobility option outside of Side and Front Dashing, Rolling, and Wall Running, and it can be very useful in a mix or combo extend, however its detriment is that it is on a 16s combo when used in neutral, leading it to be a tool that has to be used sparingly. In order to be used as a mixup option, Fluttering Pounce can be used by aiming up/over the opponent's head, and either side/back dashing to the position you were previously in when closer to the ground, you can bypass lock-on and hit behind their block. Another option is to jump as you hit the ground for a roll or front dash, acting similarly to what you can do off of Vessel's feint. Note that pressing an M1 mid Fluttering Pounce will lead to Fluttering Pounce being cancelled by the M1 and stopping all momentum, which can add to the mix by changing up the times at which you stop flying and can side/backdash to change direction or front dash. If timed correctly, pressing M1 and Fluttering Pounce in close succession, will lead to an extra M1. This can be done with an uppercut leading to a double uppercut, via: 3xM1 + Uppercut + Look up + Fluttering Pounce + Hold M1, which can lead to a Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant.

Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant is Locust Guy's main (only) gimmick and combo extender, and is a core part of his kit. Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant can be used after and uppercut surf for increased damage. If timed correctly, an M1 can be used once before using Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant in order to do 3 M1s in the air instead of the regular 2 M1s (and is used in the "Heavy Combo" Mentioned by the Overview.

This tech is used to do a complete M1 reset using just Wing Throw, maximising damage and such ... Wing Throw (Aim up) M1 (x3, catch) ... Shortened DSL ... 4 (Aim up) M1 (x3, catch) ... Perhaps one of Locust Guy hardest Tech, this tech will allow an M1 reset if pulled off successfully. But there are [b]FOUR[/b] major roadblocks that stop this Tech from being consistent and easy to perform: Map, Ragdoll Physics, Directional Influence (DI), and Evasive [i]Map[/i]: This Tech is basically impossible to pull off in a map with a low ceiling as Locust Guy needs to fly up to max height and throw the opponent at the apex of Wing Throw [i]Ragdoll Physics[/i]: Ragdoll in JJS interact really weirdly with Wing Throw, and Locust Guy can't control it. Sometimes the opponent body would clip into Locust Guy during the move, making throwing the opponent straight up basically impossible [i]Directional Influence (DI)[/i]: One of the more niche and less known mechanics in JJS, A player can hold down W/A/S/D to change the flying path direction of their Air Ragdoll ever so slightly. This mechanic is majorly present in Disaster Plants counterplay, but it appears here to screw up the Tech anyway (the opponent can just influence their flying direction and make Locust Guy miss his M1s) [i]Evasive[/i]: This Tech require the opponent to have no evasive

[b]First[/b], Locust Guy needs to waste their opponent evasive while not using Wing Throw, so landing a Crushing Jaws would be ideal. A ping diff too big and this Tech is simply not doable) [b]Fourth[/b], Congratulations!!! Locust Guy has just landed one of his hardest Tech and deal major damage

Lucky Coward raise his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Sword[/color] up and slice down diagonally from left to right, dealing 12 damage and breaking Block. A follow-up barrage of attacks to Stinger, Lucky Coward repeatedly thrusts his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Sword[/color] down on the ragdolled opponent in front of him 3 times before stopping, each thrust is unblockable and deal 2 damage for a total of 6 damage. Due to the incredibly low stun time on behalf of the opponent, the move often leads to a 'scramble situation', where both the Lucky Coward and the opponent can act at the same time in very close proximity. This situation is very slightly in favour of the Lucky Coward, as they can act before the opponent. The Lucky Coward should be wary of oncoming M1s, as the opponent, having just come out of ragdoll, will not be affected by the Lucky Coward's M1s. Lucky Coward is not a particularly "techy" character perchance. But when it comes to applying some of the technical theory, he is quite consistent at it. This is due to how simple his moves synergize with each others. For example, using Backstab on wake up is a common tech that help getting Lucky Coward a combo on the opponent wake up, and it is simple and consistent enough to do it over and over again. Other more important part of his technical gameplan is to learn how to position himself and his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] for the best result and the correct way to stack moves on top of each other to apply pressure, or deal quick technically unevasivable damage. Positioning is extra important to Lucky Coward survival and overall gameplan. Due to how destruction just straight up screws with the Hand Sword pathfinding, learning to pay attention to the Sword and making the right decision while also placing yourself at the ideal spot will turn a regular Lucky Coward into a high level one. When you have played Lucky Coward for a long time and is playing him in this current version (1.81.2). You will know that Destruction is re-enabled in ranked. This is rather bad news for Lucky Coward, so here's a list of stupid fuckery that can happen to him: - Hand Sword deciding to move 100 studs away from the opponent. - Hand Sword staying still in a no debris spot because apparently 1 stud height is enough to break the pathfinding. - Hand Sword's attacks spin uncontrollably and miss when used under debris/unbreakable parts of the map. - Ankle Cutter would miss if the opponent is 1 stud below/above thanks to the debris - Ankle Cutter would miss if there is debris in the way because it makes the Sword changes it attack direction or straight up blocks it. - Cheap Shot missing due to opponent lying on broken floor because the attack does reach 1 stud below. - Debris blocking your cursor so you can't redirect/recall the Hand Sword. - Hand Sword taking its stroll through the National Park before coming back to you. Vessel tends to be a very easy matchup for Lucky Coward. In neutral, they dont really have any options against Ankle Cutter, except a well timed 1r or 2r, but it's very unreliable to dodge this way. They're just an M1 merchant and you can easily read or react to their aggressive dashes and dodge + trip/dash. About dodging, all of their moves are dodgable and the dash moves have very telegraphed startups. In case of Vessel landing an M1, their options aren't good, their best bet is to use normal Cursed Strikes as quickly as possible to give themselves i-frames and hopefully make you whiff a move, but even then, this move is punishable after it ends by either Ankle Cutter or High Time (this one less consistent), the Aerial version is also punishable by these moves. Crushing Blow surprisingly doesn't give the Vessel i-frames and can be easily punished mid-move. Black Flash is punishable with evasive into Trip, and Black Flash chaining punished by Ankle Cutter. Counters aren't good against Lucky Coward since the sword counts as an NPC and therefor Manji Kick will counter the air in case of Ankle Cutter and High Time hitting. This is not the case for Dirty Play and Cheap Shot, so keep that in mind.

This matchup is very awkward. The main reason is that Ten Shadows can just feed you to the rabbits and unable your dash when you're sword-off and hold block to either make you take 14 free damage or make you use Dirty Play (sword will probably not come in time) to reduce slightly the damage, pretty bad since it's one of your best neutral tools. Then there's Toad, which is also guaranteed to land if you're sword-off but at least this move is punishable on hit by an Ankle Cutter or High Time. And lastly, Divine Dogs, which you can react and dodge, but if Ten Shadows gets upclose to add more pressure with m1s, it becomes really hard to keep up with the tempo. There's still some room for counterplay, you can cancel Rabbit Escape, manage your cooldowns to never get forced into a combo by Toad, and Trip or use any ragdoll move against Divine Dogs (you can also play sword-on, but you're just an m1 trading vegetable against a better m1 trading character). It's a tricky matchup but playable and winnable.

Completely unwinnable for our unlucky fella. Supernova dominates the encounter since it's an "Explosion" type move, and Lucky Coward can only dodge "Melee" and "Bullet" moves, meaning there is almost no counterplay and you will be hit by it. Ankle Cutter and Dirty Play should be the saviors, but you can't add additional melee pressure since you can't approach, and even if you manage to land it, Blood Manipulator has 3 more to go. Talking about other moves, Piercing Blood is undodgable(?), which makes it a threat in neutral, and Flowing Red Scale and its aerial counterpart both can help avoid Ankle Cutter.

Black Death has an extremely favorable matchup against Lucky Coward, particularly while he is swordless. Injury makes evasive usage in Sword mode inconsistent and can quickly drain Miracles in neutral, preventing Lucky Coward from relying on the 1-Miracle evasive tech when comboed to 0 HP, further exacerbating his already low health. Flying Roach Swarm can avoid Ankle Cutter and High Time through its verticality and startup, then immediately close the gap against Swordless Lucky Coward. R Roach Swarm is also an oppressive dash bait that keeps him outside Black Death's side-dash range. Since it is an explosion-type attack and cannot be dodged, it discourages Lucky Coward from using Trip for Miracle generation or combo conversions. Detach is an unpunishable neutral poke that can take away a significant portion of Lucky Coward's health if Black Death wins the ensuing okizeme interactions. Its fast launch also makes confirming Taunts difficult, even with proper setup, while dodging the second Detach is highly inconsistent and often unreactable compared to blocking. Furthermore, both Festering Strikes and Chokehold are immune to Lucky Coward's swordless moves, limiting his ability to interrupt Black Death in neutral or during combos. Earthen Insect Trance's blindness, especially after blocking the second Detach, further compromises Lucky Coward's ability to use Dodge, Trip, and Taunt effectively. Overall, Black Death heavily suppresses Swordless Lucky Coward's neutral and resource generation, forcing him to rely on stronger fundamentals in Sword mode to find openings. This is especially difficult against a character capable of rapidly draining his Miracles and exploiting his low health.

The [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] must be dropped. Taken for granted. 2. Upon pressing G, the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] will reel back before charging forward. 3. Then it leaps. The [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] will trace a short path midair before: - 3.1 (if the enemy has been targeted by the sword with R special) changing course to target the nearby enemy; - 3.2 (if the sword hasn't been given a specific target) maintain its course and attempt to land at any enemy in its path. 4. Even then, the enemy must not be in [b]grounded ragdoll[/b] by the time the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] leaps. 5. Jawbreaker successfully strikes. - Strategies for [b]Activation[/b]: [b]NOTE:[/b] Now that, as of 1.78, its healing factor has been transferred to on-hit properties rather than whiff, Lucky Coward has no gain from using [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] outside as a last resort get-off-me button. 1. Be aware of when Lucky Coward can activate [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] defensively: lead the opponent into a situation where Lucky Coward can confirm it, such as endlag or active frames of a move, where the opponent is unable to dash away. 2. Set up [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] to attack offensively: while [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color], indeed, does not hit grounded ragdoll, it is perfectly capable of hitting an [b]aerial ragdoll[/b]. Lucky Coward has two tools to bring any ragdoll into a brief aerial state: [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Trip[/color], and [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Shoot[/color]. Timing one of these two on a ragdoll the exact moment the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] begins its leap [b]will confirm[/b] [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color]. [b]NOTE: the direction from which Lucky Coward launches the ragdoll will also be the direction of[/b] [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color][b]'s knockback.[/b] - Speaking of [b]Knockback[/b]: [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] will knock the enemy far away on hit. By the time Lucky Coward gets within range of attacking the stunned opponent, the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbroken[/color] stun will be already half-expired. This is disastrous for the damage output. Lucky Coward, though, is able to deal with this within two main contexts: [b]Near a wall:[/b] 1. The first strategy in mitigating the knockback and immediately priming Lucky Coward to make full use of the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbroken[/color] stun is to, in fact, use [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Trip[/color]/[color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Shoot[/color] to direct the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbroken[/color] opponent towards a wall to prematurely stop their travel. [b]In the open fields:[/b] 2. Fortunately, Lucky Coward's tools that aid him in confirming Jawbreaker offensively will also help him with cancelling its knockback. Indeed, timing [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Trip[/color]/[color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Shoot[/color] with the moment the enemy is knocked away, easily told by the sound cue, will cancel Jawbreaker's knockback by replacing it with [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Trip[/color]/[color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Shoot[/color]'s own.

At an introductory stage, M1 trading consists of using the fundamentals repetitively to try an eventually breach your opponents' block. Like established in the afformentioned introduction, different characters will have different advantages and disadvantages in M1 trading, with the most important thing being finesse, how well you can jump and dash around to eventually get your opponent to face the wrong direction, at the wrong time, for you to land a crucial attack.

We already talked about the kinds of character's involved. Now we are going to talk about the options within M1 trading that people tend to do. After a player blocks, they have a few options that they can choose to do. Block -> X -> Block Value M1 Fast and Effective M1 M1 The most common path Wait, M1 The wait can throw people off Side Dash M1 Good Quick Thing Side Dash M1 M1 Also good Wait, Side Dash M1 Very good for throwing people off Headjump M1 The first time in a fight, this almost 100% works These are only some examples of what can be done. Usually, everyone has a few specific pattern they stick to. We talked about how M1 trading is all about adaption, and this is where it truly shines. You must be able to understand the patterns of your opponent, and leverage them to punish them.

There are five kinds of levels to M1 trading. Level Kills M1 / Side Dash Blocking 1 0-500 Simple M1 String. Does not turn around/predict. 2 500-1k M1 once or twice. Very minimal prediction. 3 1k-3k Incorporates Side Dashing. Turns Around 4 3k-6.5k Headjump + Delayed Side Dash Fast Prediction and Risktaking 5 10k+ Leverages an assortment of techniques to penetrate block. Actively adapts and pays attention to opponent. Obviously these are not set in stone, but the kinds of techniques that an opponent leverages tells you a lot about how good they are as a player, and allows you to learn about them on the technical scale, leading me to Adaption.

M1 trading is the core staple of JJS combat, operating as the most crucial factor in determining who is objectively 'better'. It is the most important skill to build, and oftentimes, is the key deciding factor of battles, regardless of who is using which character (with the sole exception of Disaster Plants, who operates outside of JJS's usual M1 trading mechanics). In the practical sense, M1 trading is extremely simple. It is arguably a state beyond neutral, and before combos. It is the moment that both users are directly engaging with one anothers using M1s, Dashes, and most importantly, [color=hsl(100, 100%, 75%)]Blocking[/color]. At higher states and levels of the game, these exchanges tend to last for longer amounts of time, and winning them requires Adaption. Adaption in this case, is memorizing and understanding the patterns and tendencies of opponents, how they react, M1-Dash patterns, blocking directions, and infinite other factors which contribute to the rigor of M1 trading as a whole. You will have the question; "how do I improve at M1 trading?". The key answer, and probably the answer to all of your functional mechanical/intellectual problems in life, is for you to simply practice. M1 trade with others, pay attention to your mistakes, and also the other parties' mistakes. Mechanics Involved

Seperates a good M1 trader from a God Level Goated M1 trader. Adaptation is concept about how attentive you are to the patterns of your opponent. Here is a scenario examples: "What? He got past my block by delaying his M1s and the side dashing? I'll keep that in mind." Next Encounter: "He delayed his M1, and I punished that. Now he will have to concieve another method to fight me."

Perfection can adapt to situations with his R special by changing his M1s, dashes, moves and ult moves. While not being weak, Perfection still lacks some better neutral and, comparing his combo damage to other characters, Perfection gets the shorter end of the stick. Perfection benefits the most from his flexibility and versatility, having an option for nearly every situation while still being partially an M1 merchant (who isn't?). His R special still gives him some variety by giving the player three different modes of M1s to choose from. He can outshine others by adapting to the current situation and always have an option. Also, he can make an army out of transfigured humans.

[b]All-Rounding:[/b] If you don't use your R special and stay in your normal mode, then the character works the best as an M1 merchant. If use your special once and use the Blade Mode you will lose some damage for more combo potential and a dash that can catch players off guard. If you use your special twice and use the Club Mode then you will deal shorter but high damage combos that will use less moves. Once you master the dash and the M1 trading, you'll be a monster. [b]Neutral:[/b] Stockpile (Aerial) and Focus Strike (Timed) are block bypasses that have fast startup, making it good for neutral but having high endlag on whiff. Body Repel has a [i][i]long[/i][/i] start up but is a nice ranged attack that is hard to dodge because of its aimability. It is also a gap closer and a general mobility option with its 4 + 3 variant.
Due to switching after an M1 is blocked its possible to switch from the 2nd Blade M1 to deliver a block breaking 3rd Club M1
Wherever a Downslam may be fitted in a Combo theres a high chance it could be replaced for a Club Downslam for 1-2 additional damage

One of Perfection's most reliable combo extenders. Stockpile is true and safe off any M1 string, regardless of mode. Perfection can do 3 M1s > [i]Stockpile[/i] > Any move Stockpile's 2nd swing will always connect to opponents hit by the 1st swing, allowing Perfection to turn their camera and change the direction of its knockback. This behavior does not apply when the 1st swing is blocked. Stockpile's aerial ragdoll is safe from evasives, and can function as solid evasive bait if Perfection plays their cards correctly. Relying on this isn't recommended, but can work against most opponents. Take note of the opponent's evasive habits. When timed correctly after an uppercut, the first swing can connect with ragdolls. This can be safely done on opponents without evasive for extra damage. Stockpile's second swing can be used on ragdolls to confirm a Body Repel, but otherwise it's generally recommended to use its air variant. Never do this when the opponent has their evasive. The aerial ragdoll of Stockpile launches opponents high enough to land an air M1 or Focus Strike's standard variant. Ragdoll lasts long enough to land a downslam. Stockpile's highly telegraphed startup means that using it on a ragdolled opponent, grounded or not, will likely lead to an evasive punish.

Being a block bypassing move, Stockpile can be used to win M1 trades similarly to [url=https://dogslamloop.com/characters/Honored_one/index.html]Honored One[/url]'s Rapid Punches. Be wary of spacing when attempting this, as opponents close enough to Perfection are able to block the 1st swing and interrupt them with an M1 before the 2nd swing lands. Be wary of counters for the same reason. If the opponent has their sidedash available, they may be able to dash around Perfection or out of Stockpile's range entirely before the 2nd swing connects. This can result in a punish, given Stockpile's high endlag. Stockpile's surprisingly high range can catch opponents off guard, but relying on its range too much will often get Perfection punished.

Soul Fire un-like Stockpile may be punished if used after 3M1s Due to its longer range Soul Fire may be used after a back dash or moves with high knockback to lower the risk of the combo or to tag on damage after a traditional combo ender Soul Fire's ragdoll hitting properties and long range mean it can combo of any move with more stun than its startup Soul Fires noticeable startup and non ignorable block endlag means it is punishable when used from closer ranges on non true ragdolls If used while outside of the range of a side dash + M1 it may be used to bait evasive though poorly

Being a decently fast ranged move Soul Fire may substitute a side dash + M1 punish while either of those options aren't available Soul Fires long range and semi-fast startup may be used to cancel Specials or Moves usually used outside of side dash range like the Specials of Black Death or True Cannon
