Switcher is a character revolving around his burst damage and his swaps. With most of his moves being close range, he's sure to do a lot of damage if an opponent lets him win an engagement, with tools in his disposal to get in their face and start fighting. [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]Boogie Woogie[/color] is his special which can act as a way to dodge, disorient, and feint, but is best used as a catalyst for his variants. He has Swift Kick, which is a kick that comes out moderately fast into a grab that can extend his combos. His third move, Pebble Throw, is a versatile tool that's used best with his special, acting as both an approach tool and a combo extender into a move with high burst damage, like Brute Force. With the combination of his newfound combo potential, as well as an effective approach tool and evasive bait, Switcher is one hard-hitting pick for a character that mostly relies on fundamentals.[color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)][/color]

Switcher's gameplan is to get up close using [i]Pebble Throw[/i], with its two variants: [i]Blazing Star[/i] is the move that allows Switcher to glide around his opponent, letting him hit different angles fast. [i]Gut Punch[/i] is [i]Pebble Throw's[/i] second variant, which either directly puts him in an advantageous position, stunning his opponent and swapping him in front of them, or in a neutral position favored towards him if its blocked due to its low endlag. It's a high priority for Switcher to bait out evasive, as most of his moves have high enough startup to be easily punishable, which can be done with [i]Swift Kick[/i] and [s](again)[/s] [i]Pebble Throw[/i], as [i]Pebble Throw[/i] threatens a 30 damage followup.

The defining trait of Switcher that differentiates him from other characters. Boogie Woogie, with its very low startup up close, can be unpredictable against an opponent during an M1 trade, forcing them to constantly react to his swaps. It also can feint moves at any point during them, allowing him to mitigate his high whiff endlag on his moves, as well as to keep combos true, namely with [i]Elbow Drop[/i]. These are other uses for [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]Boogie Woogie[/color]: Feint mixups Combo extending after using [i]Brute Force[/i] Swapping himself or his opponent to an object made by an opponent (Lucky Coward's sword, Black Death's Earthen Insect Trance, etc.)

He can use Blazing Star, Pebble Throw's variant, to get close with his opponent. Pebble Throw can also be a good interruption tool, with its low startup and its follow-up to Gut punch. He can also use Boogie Woogie during M1 trades, in tandem with sidedashes, to gain a positional advantage. If an opponent burnt their sidedash within sidedash range, he can use sidedash and Elbow Drop as it's unblockable.

Switcher kicks his opponent, dealing 9 damage and knocking them away standing up, then goes for a grab and throws them away, dealing 1 and 9 damage respectively. His kick's startup is fast, but slow enough to be reactable after 4 M1s, with his grab coming out relatively fast after landing the kick, usually guaranteeing you hit the grab after the kick. His grab can also be aimed from straight up to straight down, opening for a lot of unique combos.

Switcher starts sliding straight into the opponent, dealing 7.5 damage. The Switcher then follows up with a kick straight up on the opponent, dealing 7.5 damage. The moves has a fast startup, but it comes at the cost of being unsteerable during the kick. Switcher, during the slide, is in a ragdolled state, and can only be hit by moves that hit ragdoll. If the opponent is ragdolled, the kick isn't done.

Switcher winds up for a moment before delivering a devastating punch, dealing 17.5 damage. The punch comes out with enough force for the wind gust to blow the opponent away if they're not close enough, dealing 6 damage. The move has a slow startup, with moderate whiff endlag.

During Blazing Star, Switcher can use Brute Force to wind up a devastating kick, essentially doing the same thing as base Brute Force. However, if Brute Force is pressed again with correct timing, Switcher can hit a black flash, dealing 24 damage and knocking them away.

Switcher kicks up and punches a pebble, dealing 4 damage if it hits an opponent, and lingers for 1.5 seconds if whiffed. This move's utility comes from what Switcher can do after throwing the pebble, being able to swap with the pebble for movement, or to swap in front of his opponent to attack them. This move has relatively high startup, with options right after using it.

Switcher charges up an uppercut, dealing 5 damage, before slamming down on their opponent with their elbow, bouncing them up [s]sometimes[/s] and dealing 7 damage. This move has moderate startup, with a very long lingering active hitbox, but a noticeable whiff endlag.

Combo damage does not account for passive regeneration. The damage of each skill was calculated using the damage modifier in a private server. Feinting a move with Boogie Woogie puts Boogie Woogie in cooldown, which locks out Gut Punch after a feinted move. Three M1s to Brute Force is green and is susceptible to counters Swapping after Brute Force is ping dependent

While it looks to be powerful in neutral, in execution, Boogie Woogie is usually unthreatening, as his followup is usually limited to M1s. Keeping this in mind, tracking and reacting to his movements while holding [BLOCK] is fine. Boogie Woogie essentially forces both targets to functionally stand still which means there's usually nothing of value, overall making Boogie Woogie a very fake neutral option. There are three ranges in which Boogie Woogie can be used: long-range, mid-range, and close-range.
This is the distance wherein Boogie Woogie is blockable. The Switcher can't extract much value out of doing this.

This is the range wherein Boogie Woogie is unblockable, but is too far to have any proper follow up. The Switcher may decide to front dash here, but with proper tracking, as well as the chase's really large whiff endlag, makes this option too unsafe.

This is the distance wherein Boogie Woogie is unblockable, and is within the range of a side-dash M1. This is usually the most disorienting and dangerous spot where Boogie Woogie can be used, but if the opponent preserves their sidedash, the startup of Boogie Woogie gives them enough time to interrupt his swap into a combo.

An [b]Archetype[/b] refers to a character’s [b]optimal playstyle[/b] and [b]type of Neutral[/b] based on their attributes/properties such as movement, move types, neutral tools, gimmicks, combo strength, and the fundamentals. Most importantly, an [b]Archetype[/b] in JJS here is defined in the context of a 1v1 ranked match [i](1v1, no Ult, first to 3, and ranked maps)[/i], so we don’t categorize the characters by their strength in a public server for example or how strong their ult are.
What is an archetype in JJS?

Being a certain Archetype does not mean a bad thing; it just describes their optimal gameplan and the way they interact in the [b]Neutral state[/b] of the game [b]Traditional Archetypes[/b] will be redefined and re-fit to make them make sense within the context of JJS (A Keep Away would not mean sitting halfway across the map sniping people down, etc.)
Awesome video showing proper approach tools being used and winning interactions at close range.

Characters with the [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]Close In Archetype[/color] often aim to play as aggressive as possible. Using a multitude of Gapcloser/Mobility and M1 Trading tools [i](Close Range Blockbreaker, Mixups, etc.)[/i] that can give the character proper advantage [u](M1 priority, Block pressure, Combo start, etc.)[/u], [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]Close In[/color] is defined by their strengths to close the distance, put pressure at close range, and win interactions at M1 to Side Dash range using the tools they have. Awesome video showing characters punishing enemy mistakes such as being interrupted by skills or having their momentum halted.

Characters with [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]Reversal Archetype[/color] have their gameplan built around capitalizing on their opponent's actions aka mistakes. These characters aren't defined by their effective range but by their ability to bait and punish with their skills [i](For example: Predicting an enemy Side Dash and going in to punish it without the need of Side Dash M1)[/i]. [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]Reversal[/color] is defined by their ability to turn around the flow of the match and to gain great value from correctly guessing and punishing their opponent mistakes. Awesome video showing zoning tools being used at a range to start a combo and the character retreating afterward.

Characters with [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]Keep Away Archetype[/color] operates at around the Side Dash to Front Dash range, their most effective range. Unlike the traditional definition, these characters are not fighting really far away or prefer to stay away all the times. While their capability upclose might be subpar compared to a [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]Close In[/color], their skills and abilities are designed to keep up the pressure at range and zone the opponent out [i](Long Range Blockbreaker, Poke, Trap, Area Denial, etc.)[/i]; then win the [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]Keep Away[/color] the game

A brother of [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]Close In[/color], characters with [color=#ff2323]M1 Merchant Archetype[/color] means that most of their skills are either combo filler [i](not worth to use in Neutral)[/i] or too weak/meaningless [i](can't convert to great value even if landed in Neutral)[/i]. Their options to engage is limited to the infamous Side Dash M1, thus their Archetype name. It is not a bad thing to be an [color=#ff2323]M1 Merchant[/color], but most of times, [color=#ff2323]M1 Merchants[/color] take up most of the weaker characters in the roster (there are exceptions of course). For more clarification, Side Dash M1 is a great tool, not that it is weak or anything, but we are excluding it from "Neutral" for the sake of making it clear.
Awesome video showing a character closing in and catching a counter attack with a skill, then proceed to maul the opponent.

A mix of [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]Reversal[/color] and [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]Close In[/color], characters with [color=hsl(319.73, 88.24%, 50%)]Oppressor Archetype[/color] prefers to close the distance with the opponent, engage with them at such distance, and look out to punish any mistake the opponent make. While they don't need to have [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]great Mobility[/color] or [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]Interruption Gimmicks[/color], it is the tools they have that define them. They can have a great Punish tool that work at Close Range, or they can put great rushdown pressure on the opponent after punishing their mistake. Otherwise known as Reversal Close In, the name is to simply shorten it. One more thing, characters of this archetype don't need to have the best quality of both the archetypes that make up it, it is their effective range that create the overlap (M1 to Side Dash Range) Note Awesome video showing a character interrupting an opponent approach option and start combo-ing them from afar.

These archetypes are meant to be added on to the Base and Mixed Archetypes defined above; they are mostly flavor texts. At most, we only allow 1 flavor archetype and 1 base archetype to go with each other, for consistency and simplicity sake.

Characters with Mixup Archetype prefer to perform mixup as part of the optimal gameplan and neutral. These mixups can either be a forced gimmick or alternative optional actions. For example, a "Mixup Close In" would prefer to rush down the opponent with their mobility and keep the pressure not by block pressure but by mixups.

Characters with Agile Archetype have multiple great option to move around the battlefield aka their mobility. Because Close In already have this quality, this is rather used to describe characters of other Archetypes who have a strong point in their mobility (to either rush down or creating distance)

Characters with Setplay Archetype prefer to do something non-combative in order to set up their gameplan, it can be buffing their moves or creating a trap. For clarification, back-loaded damage is not Setplay
Characters with Puppet Archetype are defined by their ability to control an independent entity that can move and interact with the environment.

Characters with Install Archetype are defined by their modes, in which one is clearly a lot more powerful than the other one. They usually achive this state via fulfilling a conditional or something else that stop them from achieving the mode 90% of the time.

Defined by his amazing long ranged capabilities and solid close ranged moves, True Cannon is able to do strong damage from just about any range in a fight. He has access to his defining safe and spammable projectile, Granite Blast, which can be charged to block-break and deal extra damage. Second Helping is a block-break that's extremely difficult for most characters to deal with without having access to a counter, alongside having moves like Appetizer and Unsatisfied that can lead to devastating combos when landed. Most of these moves come with the cost of having to manage a resource meter, "Overheat". True Cannon has subpar damage when overheated, and does not have access to Granite Blast or most of Appetizer's projectiles without having sufficient meter. This means he can struggle against characters that can close the distance easily when he needs to use his special, which leaves him completely vulnerable. True Cannon does have setups that allow him to somewhat consistently get out of overheat safely, but this doesn't mean that you shouldn't manage your meter to avoid Overheat. Having tools that can completely negate the M1 trading aspect of the game that most characters in the game are forced to engage in, True Cannon is easily one of the top tiers in Jujutsu Shenanigans, with hard to punish weaknesses if your character isn't able to contest his playstyle.

Passive Strat: True Cannon’s main strategy is that you wanna keep your enemy as far as you can to do safe Restyles and snipe them from a distance. You can use Second Helping to safely disengage close combat when needed. Use Granite Blast to snipe and aim at the direction they are gonna go when using charged beams and use the normal one as a poking option to bait their side dash and much more. Unsatisfied is extremely good for evasive baiting when combined with Second Helping or Appetizer and can be mixed with charged Granite Blast to safely back dash and use Restyle. Appetizer can be used to surprise your opponent due to its quiet, fast windup time. Using the Sweet variant of Restyle is a much safer option than Haircomb, but that doesn't mean you can’t be punished for using it, so watch out. Close up strat: Though True Cannon is more effective at longer ranges (because the game is full of M1 merchants) The passive Strat is uneffective against gap closers. As known to his passive, his Unsatisfied and Second Helping reduces the cooldown of his Special. Using this mechanic, True Cannon can avoid doing the Haircomb variant of Restyle, being easily punished by it, as it takes 2.75s to finish. Instead, we do the Sweet variant, which only takes 1s. By using this mechanic we can play True Cannon at its fullest potential.

When dashing, True Cannon can use Granite Blast at any point before the hit or whiff to extend their chase to around double its distance. The original chase is interrupted and the character stands still for a moment before spinning a granite blast around them as they dash forwards once again. This dash variant is still very punishable on block and has a noticeable, very visible startup. It's fairly easy to punish for an opponent expecting it, which is why it's best used sparingly as a mixup instead of crossing up with or whiffing a front dash. Because the dash lasts for a fairly long time, it can be used to bait counters and punish them. This is especially useful vs Aspiring Mangaka, who is one of True Cannon's worst matchups. It's other usage is to turn a defensive front dash into a reversal (or to move further away). This can be useful if True Cannon wasted their side-dash and now is stuck with the committal front dash to avoid moves. Another rare situation, but still a useful one if the moment comes.

Unsatisfied has True Cannon throw three quick punches before shoulder-barging their opponent and launching them away in a ragdoll. It's fast, can pick up aerial ragdolls and the barge hits grounded ragdolls too. A useful combo tool. Like its melee brother Second Helping, it restores some of True Cannon's Sweet! cooldown for each hit, meaning it's important to insert into combos to keep pressure on the opponent and keep the Overheat meter low. Importantly for its use in combos, Unsatisfied's first hits connect with aerial ragdolls and stand up the person, which means the full move (and Sweet! cooldown reduction) connect and it also makes it harder to evasive punish since it hits deceptively high in the air. The move is also a (weak) M1 interrupt. It comes out quickly enough to string as block pressure from an M1 hit on block, and looks like an M1 as well. This is not something that should be used frequently, since it's punishable if they keep blocking, but it can be useful when used sparingly.

Second Helping is a ranged, block breaking neutral skip which also has use as a combo extender/ender. The skill quickly transports its user toward a target, where they float for a small time with melee I-frames before slamming down with an unblockable punch. If it is missed, [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]True Cannon[/color][b][/b] is left floating for a small period where they can be punished. As a [b]neutral skip,[/b] Second Helping is a solid move. Any overextensions from the opponent can be punished with the move since it has a large range, and it can sometimes be hard to react to if the opponent doesn't expect it, especially since [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]True Cannon[/color][b][/b]'s kit is very blockable. However, beware that opponents who hold jump when not engaging in m1 trades or neutral [color=#524f4f](AKA everyone ever)[/color] often cause the move to hover [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]True Cannon[/color][b][/b] too high and whiff vertically, leading to the opponent's free punish. Second Helping is also a [b]combo tool.[/b] When the target is an aerial ragdoll, (e.g. after uppercut or Appetizer) the opponent's ragdoll becomes true instantly before [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]True Cannon[/color][b][/b] flies up to them, punches them downwards and ragdolls them for a short time on the ground. Because it is an instant true ragdoll, this move is decent evasive bait when it threatens after the opponent is ragdolled in the air, since its damage becomes unavoidable. It can also be used as a [b]combo ender,[/b] simply because when it hits someone in the air, [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]True Cannon[/color][b][/b] can roll on the ground and is difficult to see for the grounded opponent. However, it can be extended off of with a downward aimed Granite Blast.

Sweet! is True Cannon's main method of clearing his Overheat bar. On use, it has a short startup where Ryu is stunned in place and throws his hands forward in a taunt before removing 6 Overheat stacks (out of the maximum 10). The full animation and stun lasts for 1 second. Best used outside of punish range or whilst the opponent is in ragdoll, True Cannon players should be cautious to use this move outside of combos unless they are sure that they won't get hit with a combo for using it. Also, keep in mind that landing True Cannon's Unsatisfied or Second Helping will reduce the move's cooldown by a significant amount, so try to use it more when those moves will be available to reduce its cooldown.

When Restyle is used while in Overheat, the True Cannon player pulls out a comb and fixes their hair, clearing the Overheat bar shortly after the animation starts. The move lasts 2.75 seconds and has stun for the full duration. Restyle should not be the main way for True Cannon to clear the Overheat bar, because in most situations using the variant will net their opponent a free combo. However, against some opponents, there are situations where Restyle can become safe to use at the end of very high-damage combos since the opponent is ragdolled far from the user, giving it some application. When True Cannon does overheat (usually by mistake), the player then needs to use this variant to clear the bar as safely as possible. The main ways of doing this are by comboing into a safe Restyle setup (out of Unsatisfied or a long-range Appetizer), which lets True Cannon do this safely, or simply using it when the [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]Evasive [/color]bar is full so the damage of the resulting combo is minimal. [color=#ff4600]DO NOT use this move if it might get cancelled immediately.[/color] (e.g. in m1 trades or in sidedash range.) Since the meter only clears after a short startup, when it is cancelled early True Cannon is stuck in Overheat for the entire duration of the cooldown, and still has to safely clear it. This (in almost all scenarios) is a completely awful disadvantage situation for True Cannon and will result in painful death.
True Cannon is already a very complete character, but some simple techs can allow his character to shine in other areas as well.
True Cannon Air Combos?! Jump & Uppercut Aerial Granite Blast (aimed)
Cooler Juggle. Appetizer Aerial Granite Blast (Aimed) 2/3 (optional)

Gojo can punish just about every single one of your moves, regardless of if you're careful with your usage of it or not. Has access to a teleport that punishes your comb, hell, you don't even need to overheat, as Gojo can use 2R to perform an interruption variant on your Sweet, making every usage of your special a risk for as long as he has Limitless.

[u][b]DO NOT USE YOUR SPECIAL IF HE ISN'T RAGDOLLED.[/b][/u] Be mindful of Gojo's evasive before doing just about any move or special at any range. Try to keep track of Gojo's Limitless cooldown before making any bold plays. The matchup is in your favor for as long as Gojo doesn't have Limitless ready for use. Take advantage of Gojo's subpar mobility and M1-Merchant nature and try to keep a comfortable range away from him.
How should you approach this matchup?

Yuji is an incredibly mobile character, who's able to easily close the distance between him and Ryu. At his core, he is an M1 Merchant, but this does not come with having an easier time than the rest of the cast. Yuji can effectively jump over any grounded charged Granite Blasts by using aerial 1R, as well as counter Second Helping and uncharged Granite Blasts if thrown out in neutral. Also capable of moving fast enough to punish using your comb, so overheating is quite discouraged against Yuji if they aren't absurdly far away from you.

Generally Yuji's gameplan is to throw himself at you with his mobility, so playing passively and going for punishes is optimal. Conditioning Yuji to start using counter for uncharged Granite Blasts could be helpful, as Yuji is unable to counter charged Granite Blasts. Mixing up between charged and uncharged could lead to Yuji not only wasting a counter, but also taking 14 damage. Yuji's mobility options give him the verticality to avoid grounded Granite Blasts. Unfortunately for Yuji, aerial Granite Blast has omnidirectional aim and negates this weakness of Granite Blast. Yuji's subpar health makes combos much more devastating for him to get hit by, so be sure to capitalize on every possible mistake with optimal punishes. Be mindful of your overheat bar. If usage isn't careful, Yuji has a chance to catch up.
How should you approach this matchup?

Restless Gambler is characterized by possessing limited effective mobility and a heavy reliance on close quarter combat to score meaningful damage. Being unable to approach against True Cannon is usually an unwinnable matchup for the opposing player. However, Restless Gambler does possess some useful tools for this particular matchup. Restless Gambler's Reserve Balls + Shutter Doors variant is uniquely suited to punish True Cannon at range. As such, True Cannon's Sweet, Granite Blast, and Appetizer can be punished in certain circumstances. Restless Gambler's Door Guard can be used to counter neutral Second Helping, and block charged Granite Blasts. Unfortunately, the best it can do against Granite Blast is block the attack; the Hakari is still left in punishable endlag. However, if True Cannon plays intelligently, even Restless Gambler's small counterplay can be negated entirely.

In order to take full advantage of Restless Gambler's weak approach capabilities, a True Cannon should stay at range as best they can. Door Guard's ability to block Second Helping can be negated by simply missing the hit of Second Helping as a method of coutnerbaiting. A Restless Gambler with evasive can evasive punish extremely telegraphed attacks from Granite Blast and Appetizer with the Reserve Balls + Shutter Doors variant. As True Cannon, it is much safer to simply use these moves on a standing Restless Gambler to prevent this from happening. Tracking the cooldown of Restless Gambler's Reserve Balls + Shutter Doors variant can help you decide when it is fully safe to pursue certain combo routes and neutral options. Restless Gambler's Reserve Balls + Shutter Doors variant has a fairly short range. If you are looking to safely use Sweet, just exit the effective range of this variant.
How should you approach this matchup?

Against [color=#000000]megumi[/color] you should always know that he always has tools to reach you when using [color=#FFA500]haircomb[/color], so dont use [color=#FFA500]haircomb[/color] if u dont wanna get punished. You can counter his [color=#000000]rabbit escape[/color] by using [color=#90D5FF]appetizer[/color] since the move becomes unreactable due to [color=#000000]rabbit escape[/color] hiding the quiet wind up. You can also use [color=#90D5FF]second helping[/color] once he closes the distance with rabbit escape. If [color=#000000]megumi[/color] uses his R special make sure to ALWAYS back off because he has his [color=#000000]rabbit escape[/color] variant that you cannot react to. The [color=#000000]megumi[/color] will cancel the R once you waste your backdash so you should use your [color=#90D5FF]second helping[/color], its a really really good tool in m1 trades. Lets say [color=#000000]megumi[/color] caught you, and now you dont know how to counter his safe evasive bait. You should do evasive + appetizer to catch him if they backdash and used nue + toad and got far away. [color=#000000]megumi[/color] can also use nue mid m1 trades so be careful and dodge it.
Mahito has it bad. He has poor mobility during neutral, and he cannot punish any usage of Ryu's special except with tickle-worthy damage with Soul Fire.

Bully Mahito's poor performance against players who run away from him. He has no way to catch up as long as you are cautious for his Blade Mode's front dash. Don't let that shiny "Unloseable" label fool you, you can still be put in devastating combos if you aren't careful with your spacing. Use Granite Blast to evasive punish Black Flash into Soul Fire, alongside a front dash afterwards.
How should you approach this matchup?
Although Ryu's zoning has further of a range than Choso, this matchup is still largely skill dependent.

Do not approach Choso. When you are inside of his effective range, it is much deadlier than yours. Try your best to disperse of his activated blood orbs by hitting him with a ranged attack like Granite Blast; also keeping your distance.
How should you approach this matchup?

Even though Todo is normally not an outstanding character, he surprisingly holds his own against the likes of Ryu. Swaps are great at disorientating Ryu's neutral pokes, and his Pebble Throw is great at punishing combing. Surfing on the pebble with Pebble Throw and having to mostly respect Ryu's zoning, this makes the matchup quite skill dependent for both players.

Overheating is rather situational against Todo, as his mobility with Pebble Throw makes combing risky at times. Take a careful look at where Todo is looking before a swap is done. A common tactic Todo players use is turning backwards before swapping, causing the victim to become disorientated when it's done. You can quickly do a 180 after the swap to quickly ready yourself.
How should you approach this matchup?

Genuinely [color=#895129]Higuruma[/color] cant do anything much against [color=#90D5FF]Ryu[/color] because of how unfair this matchup is. [color=#90D5FF]Ryu[/color] can just avoid engaging with backdash when [color=#895129]Higuruma[/color] uses his R special and just avoid all his melle moves and mix-ups by using [color=#90D5FF]Second Helping[/color]. The only move that properly hit you is [color=#895129]Higuruma's[/color] [color=#895129] Judgement's Reach[/color], which you can still just do backdash and use [color=#90D5FF]Second Helping[/color]. On top of all of this [color=#895129]Higuruma[/color] has 90 HP instead of 100.

Genuinely a victim to Ryu. What little neutral options Nanami has are effectively useless, as Ryu's Granite Blast can cancel moves like Blunt Cut. Due to Nanami's combos being mostly green, Ryu has chances to use Second Helping as a melee counter in the middle of combos.

Make it apparent that you are willing to cancel any raw moves thrown out in neutral by Nanami. Make combos for him as hard as possible; Second Helping has melee immunity during the windup. Nanami is an M1 Merchant as his core, so treat him as such; there's no need to approach him when he cannot deal with your superior range.
How should you approach this matchup?

As True Cannon being at most effective form in long-ranged combat, and the [i]ONLY [/i]thing he can do in long ranged combat is charged since the Aspiring Mangaka has eye-cachting that is an infinite counter. The only way you can fight is through hand-to-hand combat which Apsiring Mankaga has [b]EXTREME ADVANTAGE[/b] at. BIG TIP: Just pray you dont have to face one.

True CAnnon move Aspiring MAnkaga counter-move Granite Blast Eye-Catching Granite Blast Charged None (Thank god) Want a go?(Longer dash) Sacrilice, Shut-up Unsatisfied WHole kit Second helping Eye-catching Appetizer Eye-catching [i]So technicaly don't[/i]
Why you should NOT fight an Aspiring Mangaka
This matchup plays extremely similarly to Choso, although Mei Mei trades some neutral options for being able to stay up close better.
If Mei Mei gets you into disadvantage state, it's basically over.

Vessel first strike a pose with 30f startup, upon inputing the skill. Then the user will lunge forward around 28-32 studs, while a projectile hitbox spawned in a travel at the same speed; Notably, the user can not curve the skill, and the hitbox is active for 55f. On whiff, Vessel suffers a -25f whiff endlag; On block, Vessel instead suffers a -46f block endlag. Finally, on hit, Vessel gain 113f of Self Stun and inflict 161f of Target Stun during and after the attack barrage; this give Vessel a +48f Advantage against the target.
[color=hsl(0, 80%, 30%)]DO NOT[/color] use this skill in Neutral. The move is extremly easy to interrupt on prediction or even reaction thanks to its lengthy 30f startup.

Especially when you risk getting the move blocked and get a massive 46f block endlag, which anyone with half a braincell can punish it. Plus the fact that, you just also wasted your best damaging tool and mixup option.

Cursed Strikes exist solely to do combo and nothing else, dealing a decent 17.5 damage, and it lasts pretty long too, which can help with [b]Cooldown Stalling[/b]. Plus, it is the only safe move in Vessel's kit
As mentioned earlier, the skill on hit last quite long, so it would be decent in stalling cooldown.

It is so stupid for anyone to attempt to throw this move out of Neutral. And that's when this 'strategy' be viable with three layers of asterisk. The idea is that it is so stupid, that it becomes a suprise option that you can get away [b]if it lands[/b]. It is kinda similar to Locust Guy's 'Clever Mixup' but inferior in everyway
Beside being an extremly generic Grab move that deal damage and stall cooldown. This skill has nothing of notes that would be helpful for the user to know
This is all Melee type, so watch out for enemies move that give them Melee Iframes, you don't want to waste your skill. Furthermore, it is also very counterable (obviously).

Cursed Strikes on Hit will give Vessel Melee and Bullet Iframes for the total duration equal to the self stun. This, however, means that the skill can be diffed [b]even on Hit[/b] by uncancellable delayed Explosion moves such as Cursed Partners' Outburst or Blood Manipulator's Blood Mine.
Only Melee and Bullet Iframes on Hit

Cursed Strikes drops like an anvil on anyone trying to block or wake up from the floor, crashing straight through Vessel's enemies block to deal heavy damage while trading unsafety for pure block breaking. Vessel leaps up and drives a downward dropkick straight into the floor, slamming whoever gets in the way for 14 damage. While this move is unblockable, bypasses ragdoll, and disables lock-on, it is interruptible, cannot be feinted after downward motion or aimed straight down being heavily punishable on whiff and if Vessel's opponent has evasive, and runs on a 14-second cooldown. Serving as incredible finish tool. But often being used for fast movement for after feinting the move.

Crushing Blow charges cursed energy in Vessel's hand to slam the floor, grabbing nearby opponents by the torso and smashing them down twice before throwing them skyward. Vessel slams the opponent to the ground, grabbing nearby enemies to smash them down twice before tossing them upward for 12 total damage (6 per slam), or releasing a lower-damage shockwave for 3 damage if no target is grabbed. While this move is unblockable and bypasses ragdoll, it is interruptible during startup, having an incredibly small hitbox, often fails to drive the opponent upward if debris are around, and runs on a 15-second cooldown. Often being used as a green M1 reset

Crushing Blow dashes across the mid-air creating spacing slamming down to grab targets and perform ground slams, functioning as a airborne combo tool. Vessel dashes through the air to slam down on enemies, executing the same ground slam sequence as normal Crushing Blow for 12 total damage (6 per slam) or releasing a 3 damage shockwave on miss. While this move bypasses ragdoll, it is blockable from all sides and interruptible, but allows Vessel to feint during the initial hop to gain good amount of forward air movement and drive forward for great mobility, sitting on a 15-second cooldown.

Divergent Fist winds back Vessel's arm to throw a heavy physical strike that is quickly followed by a second, delayed wave of cursed energy to knock the enemy away. Vessel winds back their arm to deliver a blow before a second burst of cursed energy triggers, dealing 10 total damage (5 per hit). While the initial hit is blockable, the move is semi-blockable, interruptible, and partly bypasses ragdoll because the second unblockable burst bypasses shields—making it uniquely effective for punishing opponents who block all the time. Additionally, if the delayed cursed energy interrupts an opponent's action, it triggers the Interruption Variant, which bypasses ragdoll, becomes unblockable, deals 5 damage, and stuns the target briefly instead of sending them flying, all on an 18-second cooldown.

Black Flash pulls Vessel's fist back while their body flashes white, releasing a strong strike that blasts the target away upon timing a second input. Vessel pulls back their fist and flashes white, releasing, high-impact punch on a second key press to deal 10 base damage and send enemies flying. While this move is unblockable, interruptible, and cannot bypass ragdoll, it functions mainly as a solid combo tool that rewards sharp timing—doubling its impact to 20 damage if it successfully interrupts an enemy's active move (excluding blocking)—all running on a same 18-second cooldown. But being Really easy to punish on evasive.

Black Flash Chain strikes Vessel's opponent's back with cursed sparks to stun them in place, keeping the move available to unleash up to four consecutive Black Flashes in a row. Vessel connects with an opponent's back, stunning them instead of knocking them down and allowing up to four continuous strikes, ending in a heavy finisher. The initial strikes deal 7 damage (14 on interruption) while the fourth blow deals 15 damage, resetting Vessel's side dash cooldown after each successful chain hit. While this variant is unblockable, interruptible, features true ragdoll, and cannot bypass ragdoll, it is used far more often than normal Black Flash to pull off stylish combos, though it is extremely easy to punish and becomes very unreliable against decent players who know how to react, all operating on an 18-second cooldown.

Manji Kick raises Vessel's arm and leg to adopt a defensive stance, parrying incoming strikes into a sharp upward Taido roundhouse kick or swooping aerial counter. Vessel enters a guarded posture to evade incoming attacks, striking back with an upward roundhouse kick on melee hit to knock the target sideways, or spinning through the air to close distance and strike if an bullet projectiles hits Manji Kick Vessel's leaps in the air to kick the opponent. Dealing 8.5 damage, this attack is unblockable, bypasses ragdoll, features true ragdoll, can hit secondary enemies caught in the path, and operates on a 0.6s counter window. While it stands as a decent counter option in Vessel's kit, it cannot be feinted, leaving Vessel vulnerable if baited, sitting on a 20-second cooldown.

Hello! Welcome to the Writing Guide of Dogslamloop Wiki. Here, you will learn about the basics of writing things for the wiki. Or maybe you are here to remind yourself of the Guide. Either way, this Writing Guide aims to create a baseline for every articles in the wiki, a standard of Dogslamloop.

While this Guide sets up a baseline for every article to follow, individual character pages might have some difference in the tones they use or the way they format information. You can say it is a "vibe" of those character pages. Anyway, so long as these tones don't undermine or break the baseline set by the Guide, they are fine to stay; and if you want to contribute, you should also consider following the tone set by those who come earlier (Inconsistent tones would be ground for rejection, unless you plan to change the entire page)

Try to avoid personal and casual language Speak as though you're objectively correct and are the authority. Don't use words like "basically" or "idk" and the like Avoid speaking in first person (using the 'I' or 'me' pronoun) [b]As much as possible[/b], avoid addressing the player directly. Say "Honored One can combo" instead of "You can combo" You can joke around a little bit but don't get to the point where information is bogged down by humor Refer to the character as their [b]in-game JJS name[/b] ([s]Yuji[/s], Vessel) Please capitalize proper nouns ([s]granite blast[/s], Granite blast) Writing should be treated like writing professionally, but not over the top. Something on the level of High School/College essay would be high enough for the site While AI-generated text and media are banned, you can still use AI-assisted text (correcting grammar, correcting tones, etc.) [b]Do not use hateful language, slurs, discriminatory terms, and similar things. Use your common sense[/b]

It would also be good that when talking about a skill or something in a Base kit of a character, you should try your best to not mention ult (with the exception of ult bar). Especially when the site allows for switching between base and ult movesets

Beside the character pages, every other pages that are open to edit publicly on the site should follow a strict uniform technical tone instead. You can mention or refer to the reader in those pages as well as they concern something else that is not a character (Fundamentals, HUD, Frame Data, Private Server Setting, etc.)

Usage of undefined Buzzwords that are not in the Terminologies Page (Punch Kick Merchant, Ragdoll Kicker, etc.) Wrong usage of terms in Terminologies (Head of the Hei is a Zoner, Linking Blood Edge after an Uppercut is a popular Tech, etc.) Disregard for following the basics of the Guide (I personally would use this xyz combo, etc.) Usage of non-technical/troll medias (Using Medias that don't follow the Guide) Troll Submission (Repeated offenses might get you barred from submitting) Inconsistent tones Putting outdated information (Cursed Strikes can M1 reset, etc.) Making technical claims with zero to little backing/evidence (You can evasive punish Lapse Blue on Hit, etc.) Bad Grammar & Spelling ([color=hsl(0, 100%, 80%)]Veesel[/color] cna destroyly kill [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Luck Coward[/color], etc.)

Depending on the tab that you are editting, there might be some small changes to the options presented to you, those will be addressed indivdually in this guide. This section serve as a general guide on how to use the editor of Dogslamloop Wiki. Image description Here, the main components are: [b]Workspace Header[/b] [b]Workspace Navigation[/b] [b]Workspace[/b] [b]Workspace Footer[/b] [b]Preview Panel[/b]

Image description Image Description In this part, you can spot 6 functions: [b][i]Cancel, Drafts, Sync/Save, Find & Replace, Diff View, and Submit[/i][/b]. You can also see [b][i]Hub[/i][/b] and a Collapse Button to save space. For Mobile Users, you can also see the [b][i]Show Preview[/i][/b] Button. "[b]Cancel[/b]" cancels whatever you are doing and bring you back to the latest page you are in or the page you are editting, Auto-save will fire and save what you are doing. "[b]Drafts[/b]" is where you will find all of your Drafts that you either save manually or Auto-saved. You should know that Drafts are locally saved, which means that if you have your browser clear its cache, you will lose all your Drafts. Each Drafts will briefly tell you which tab and page you are editting and give you the options to either resume it or discard it. "[b]Sync/Save[/b]" is the manual save button for your Drafts. However, its secondary function "[b]Sync[/b]" only apply to Frame Data editting (see more in the Frame Data tab). You just need to know that when you are editting a skill's metadata, stats, or/and frame data, you will need to use this button to see your changes in the preview panel. Image description "[b]Find & Replace[/b]" is self-explanatory. You find certain words here, know where they are, and can choose to replace them with another word. "[b]Diff View[/b]" is an alternative way of seeing your changes compared to the Live Page. "[b]Submit[/b]" is where you submit your edit to the reviewers team to check. Here's a few things can happen: "I can't submit!": You probably haven't logged in to the site yet or you are barred from making edit for whatever reason. "Nothing is happening!": You should check your internet speed and see if it is fine or not. "I can't confirm and upload!": You should fill up the QA with proper reasoning and changelog of whatever that you have edited. Filling the QA with junks/unrelated things can be ground for [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]rejection[/color]. Image description Image description

This form has 3 types to choose from: Short, Long, and Technical. All of them would ask you to upload an optional [i]evidence[/i] field, you can leave them blank if needed; of course, filling the field with junks/unrelated things can also be ground for [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]rejection[/color] Short QA: You have a word limit of 50, be simple and succint here. Long QA: You now have a word limit of 500, go on with your reasonings and such for your changes. Technical QA: Along side a word limit of 500, you can now choose your [i]Confidence Level[/i], which ranges from Low - Mid - High. They are meant to complement your evidence level of trustworthiness/accuracy.

Image description Depend on which tab you are editting, this part will change accordingly. If you are editting a Character Page, all the Character Page tabs will appear here for you to navigate through them. Going deeper, if you are editting a Matchup tab, all the Matchup sections will appear individually here; or if you are editting non-Character Page, you can navigate through all Tabs and Sections and create or delete them as well.

Image description This is your main place in the editor. Here you can edit the content of the Page, including but not limited to Layout, Metadata, Stats, Frame Data, Blocks contents, etc. For more specific information on each individual Blocks, you can check out the "Blocks" tab in the Writing Guide. Image description A few general tools you can use here are: [b][i]Undo/Redo, Clear All, and the Block Folder feature[/i][/b] [b]Undo/Redo[/b]: Self-explanatory, you can undo mistakes, or redo accidental undo. You can also use the short key combs Ctrl + Z/Ctrl + Y to perform the actions. [b]Clear All[/b]: Clear every content in that section for you. [b]Block Folder[/b]: This is only for the editor. In a very long page full of content, you can use this feature to organize the Blocks into folders for better navigation within the workspace.

Image description Image description This is where you can Add Block to the Workspace to work on. Again, for more specific information on each individual Blocks, you can check out the "Blocks" tab in the Writing Guide. But also the Media Library. [b]Media Library[/b]: Where you upload and use medias to/for the wiki, expanded on in the "How to upload and use my medias?" section below. There are a plethora of formatting options for you in the Footer as well, all of these have their own custom styling rules in the site (they all follow this format "[option]Text[/option]"): [b]Bold[/b]: Short key comb is [kbd]Ctrl + B[/kbd] [i]Italic[/i]: Short key comb is [kbd]Ctrl + I[/kbd] [u]Underline[/u]: Short key comb is [kbd]Ctrl + U[/kbd] [s]Strikethrough[/s]: Short key comb is [kbd]Ctrl + 5[/kbd] [code]Inline Code[/code]: No short key comb [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperlink]Hyperlink[/url]: Short key comb is [kbd]Ctrl + K[/kbd] [url=#sec-discussion]Anchor[/url]: Link to a section in the same page, no short key comb [kbd]Key Inputs[/kbd]: Similar to Inline Code, but this one is built for short texts, no short key comb [noauto]No Auto[/noauto]: Disable the auto-coloring engine of the site ([noauto]Vessel, Startup[/noauto]), no short key comb [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]Color[/color]: Choose your favourite color to make your page fancy here, no short key comb

Image description Show what you are editting and how it will look if it got to the Live Page. For Frame Data, remember to click on [b]Sync/Save[/b] to actually preview your changes. A few notes: The editor is still in the process of fine-tuning and such. So, changes are expected. But the current features won't change, it is more like adding new features, and QOLs.

Step 3: Choose the stuff you want to up, please follow the guideline to upload medias (you will be reminded first time when opening Media Library, and can be revisited in the terms of service) Step 4: Yay! Stats are designed to hold any pair of Keys and Values (Handsome? Yes, Rushdown? False, ...). But here are some of the must-have Stats to have: Archetype: Rushdown? Reversal? etc. Difficulty: Very Easy/Easy/Moderate/Hard Health: 100? 85? etc. There can be extra optional Stats. Here's the allowed extra optional Stats as of now: Base Only: Yes (Full character do not have this Stat) Overpowered Character: Yes (Same rule for non-OP characters) Availability: No Longer in the Game (Apply to those who know)

Difficulty refer to the skill floor of the character. More specifically, the amount of time/skill required to learn AND use that character effectively at a beginner level. Simply knowing the kit would not count as mastering the skill floor for example. [i]Very Easy[/i]: This character is really simple and intuitive to use, so long as you have the knowledge and experience with the basic fundamentals of the game (Side Dash M1, Combo-ing, etc.) [i]Easy[/i]: This character is simple to understand and to make sense of/get used to. Though you would need something other than your basic knowledge of the fundamentals to use this character effectively such as learning the things that character can do. [i]Moderate[/i]: This character requires some amount of time before you can start to use their kit effectively. But knowing most of the fundamentals can help you out during the learning phase or even carry you through using this character, as they are not that complex/hard to get used to. [i]Hard[/i]: This character is an unintuitive one to use for anyone trying them out, it can either be a complex kit or some forced gimmick check that raise the entry bar. You can mix the difficulty adjacent to each other as needed. For example, Easy-Moderate or Moderate-Hard

This section is mostly flavor texts meant to complement the Overview, so there is no need to go in details here. As a general rule of thumb, make sure to write an element of this part like this: [kbd][b]Some keywords[/b]: General description, blah blah blah[/kbd] Image description Alternatively, if you prefer it to be more casual/friendly: [kbd]Short description and such[/kbd] Image description

Obviously, you should go over the strengths of the character in this section, but don't go in details about their kit. However, you can also describe other aspects of the character that can hook readers in learning about them such as The way they fight, How it feels to play them, etc.

Again, you should go over the weaknesses of the character in this section. Though, you can also mention other negative aspects such as The way they fight, How it feels to play them, etc. (the same ideas as above but make it seems like something that would drive the readers away)

Image description Image description Image description The overview should cover overarching concepts of what the kit is designed to do and what the appropriate way to play the character is. The Crow Charmer and True Cannon page hold the gold standard for character overviews. Briefly tells you about the weaknesses and strengths of a character, how they function, what potential they have, and do so in a way that is engaging to read. Non-repetitive language and a prose that's extremely easy to read. What [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]NOT[/color] to write, overall just way to vague and talks too opinionated rather than factual. Don't mention what "tier" they are in and don't say basic things like "they are bad". Every character in this game has enough to talk about to go in depth about playstyle for a few paragraphs at least
How to write a good Overview

This section should cover the over-arching gameplan and gameplay of the character being written about. A good [i]General Strategy[/i] should not go into details about everything or specific things. But it should communicate enough, so that the average reader can grasp most of the overall picture of the character gameplan after reading it. Furthermore, it is recommended that you use [b]Extra Sections[/b] to go into details regarding specific stuff that can't be covered in other tabs. What [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]NOT[/color] to write, overall it is the same ideas as the Overview.
How to write a good General Strategy

In the Overview & Strategy tab for each character, they will always have Character Profile, Character Overview, Playstyle, and General Strategy sections. This can't be changed ot altered in any way and extra section is an optional section authors can choose to add if needed.

You would use it to cover an aspect of the character that can't be covered in other tabs. The prime example would be Passives: innate ability of a character that alter their appearance, or give them a new mechanic. Here's the list of [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]possible and permitted[/color] topics to create an extra section for: Passive Abilities Character-specific Mechanics Character-specific Strategies Clarification regarding wordings used to describe the character (Why is my favourite Star Rage an M1 Merchant?) In-depth Guide that concern the whole character Character Design Youtubers Sponsorship List of notable Combos List of notable Techs Here's the list of [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]not permitted[/color] topics to create an extra section for: Detailed Combo write-up Detailed Techs write-up Skills' explanation Matchups Counterplay Unrelated things to the character Of course, these are fully optional and not needed for a character page to be considered completed.

When recording these things, make sure to only use the allowed skins (basic or not): Showcasing Skills/M1s/Specials/Passives Taking portraits Showcasing Combos/Techs in a Private Server or Custom Server (You can use your own skins here, but it is highly [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]discouraged[/color]) Showcasing Emotes/Other Stuff Image description As a general rule, all videos must be in webm form. They must be clear and can be viewed normally (mid to high res, no blur or laggy frame, etc.). They should also be exported at 720p (1280x720). A clip on a page is never shown wider than about 800px, so 1080p only makes it heavier and slower to load. Try to keep each clip under 2 MB; the Media Library will ask before uploading anything bigger. About map usages: Make sure to only be in the [b]Base JJS Map or a flat Grass map[/b]. Recommended locations for recording Combos/Techs are either under the Twin Towers or behind the Metro Station. Failing to follow these can be ground for [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]rejection[/color].

When recording these things, any skins are allowed (you don't have to strictly follow the list, but if you can, that would be appreciated): Doing Stuff/Combos/Techs in a Ranked/Casual match Playing around in Public Server, Roulette, Creator Clash, or Custom Servers Showcasing Stuff/Combos/Techs in a PS+ Spar (Completely different from showcasing normally in PS+; this time you need to fight the opponent and such) About map usages: Most of these scenarios already have their maps set (Ranked and Casual have Duels' maps; Roulette/Creator Clash/Custom Servers all have their own maps, ...). So for PS+ Spar, you can use any maps as well (perferably 1v1 maps, I know sparring in Base Map suck)
Image description Each character will have their own Combos tab. It will consist of three main parts: Read First, Combo Groups, and Combo Lists.
How to work with the Combos Tab

[b]Read First[/b] is where you clarify about the details of the Combos tab such as how damage are calculated, what's the thing to looks out for when performing these combos, etc. You should use this part both as an introduction to that character combo game, and a caution sign to a few things before going in.

In here, you can create as many groups as needed with the naming of your choice. In each group, you can create a [b]Combo Card[/b]; it contains the combo name, combo short description, long description, damage value, and a showcase video. The basic idea here is that, these cards will have the combos that are the main highlights for the group they belong in such as "Beginner Combos". It is recommened to create 3 Combo Groups as your starting point: [b][i]Beginner Combos, BnB Combos, and Advanced Combos[/i][/b]. Anything more than that is up to your choice, your reasoning, and the staff team decision.

In here, you will be able to create multiple tables about combos. The table have a title (aka starter) to indicate what is the move used to start a combo (it can be more flexible than this if you want). Because it is a table, you are recommended to put all possible combo routes concerning each table titles. For more details on what to enter in each fields, read below.

[b]The Long version[/b]: [i][Move Name] (Optional side text) > [Move Name] > ...[/i] <-> Name is Default DSL (Notation) Basically, you put the move name down and link between each moves with the '>' symbol. You can attach a set of notes next to move in a pair of parenthesis. You can also use '...' as a way to express that the player are free to do anything else after the combo is over or as a way to express that the combos happen in the middle of something else. Examples: Optional notes M1 (x3) Downslam Crushing Blow Cursed Strikes m1 (x3) ... A popular green M1 reset that you can pull off anytime during a Lucky Coward combo ... Sidedash Backstab (Backhit) M1 (x3) ... Another general rule is that if a move name has [b]more than 14 characters (not counting space/white space)[/b], it should be notated with its input key: NO M1 (x3) Uppercut Spatial Transferrence (Up) Air Updraft Spatial Transferrence (Forward) Flock Dive-bomb This is more like it M1 (x3) Uppercut R (Up) Air Updraft R (W) Flock Dive-bomb Here's how to write almost all universal inputs and sequence in the game: M1: Either [b]M1[/b] - [i]one M1 input/singular M1[/i], [b]M1 (x2)[/b] -[i] two M1 inputs[/i], or [b]M1 (x3)[/b] - [i]three M1 inputs[/i] Uppercut: [b]Uppercut[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be [b]Surf[/b] for [u]Uppercut Surf[/u] or [b]Headbalance[/b] for [u]Uppercut Headbalance[/u] or more[/i] Downslam: [b]Downslam[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be anything particularly worthy or more[/i] Space: [b]Jump[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be anything particularly worthy or more; Use this notation sparingly, everyone know when to jump[/i] R: [b][Special name][/b] ([i]Notes[/i]), or [b]R[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be anything particularly worthy or more[/i] Q: Either [b]Side Dash[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]), [b]Front Dash[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]), or [b]Back Dash[/b] ([i]Notes[/i])- [i]Notes can be anything particularly worthy or more[/i] 1, 2, 3, 4: Either [b][Skill name][/b] ([i]Notes[/i]), or [b]1/2/3/4[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be ... you get the point[/i] Skill variants: Either [b][Variant name][/b] ([i]Notes[/i]), or [b][Input sequence][/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) Wait/Unknown Starter/Unknown Ender: [b]...[/b] - [i]Signify the action of waiting, or to display a Combo that start in the middle of another combo/tech/something. Hence the unknown starter/ender[/i] [b]The Short version[/b]: [i][Move Input] (Optional side text) > [Move Input] > ...[/i] <-> Name is Shortened DSL (Notation) Basically, it is the same as Default DSL notation, but you would only want to write out the input. [u]Do not[/u] write move name when using this notation style. Here's how to write almost all universal inputs and sequence in the game M1: Either [b]M1[/b] - [i]one M1 input/singular M1[/i], [b]M1 (x2)[/b] -[i] two M1 inputs[/i], or [b]M1 (x3)[/b] - [i]three M1 inputs[/i] Uppercut: [b]UC[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be [b]Surf[/b] for [u]Uppercut Surf[/u] or [b]Headbalance[/b] for [u]Uppercut Headbalance[/u] or more[/i] Downslam: [b]DS[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be anything particularly worthy or more[/i] Space: [b]J[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be anything particularly worthy or more; Use this notation sparingly, everyone know when to jump[/i] R: [b]R[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be anything particularly worthy or more[/i] Q: Either [b]SD[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]), [b]FD[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]), or [b]BD[/b] ([i]Notes[/i])- [i]Notes can be anything particularly worthy or more[/i] 1, 2, 3, 4: [b]1/2/3/4[/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) - [i]Notes can be ... you get the point[/i] Skill variants: [b][Input sequence][/b] ([i]Notes[/i]) Wait/Unknown Starter/Unknown Ender: [b]...[/b] - [i]Signify the action of waiting, or to display a Combo that start in the middle of another combo/tech/something. Hence the unknown starter/ender[/i] Examples: M1 (x3) UC (Surf) 1 2 R 3 4 (Miss) R (Activation) M1 (x3) DS 4 (Summon) M1 (Whiff) 4 (Swipe) M1 (x2 + Whiff) DS [b]You should also use these combo notation for Techs notation as well[/b]

Image description The main parts: [i]Name[/i]: The combo name [i]One Line[/i]: A short one-sentence description of the combo [i]Route[/i]: You enter the route here. [b][i]MAKE SURE THAT THE INPUTS ARE PER LINE[/i][/b] like this [code]M1 (next line) M1 (next line) Skill 1[/code] unlike the Combo Block [i]Damage[/i]: The total damage the combo would do to an opponent with zero damage reduction; as a general rule, combo damage would not count passive regeneration but you can clarify that as needed in the Write Up [i]Difficulty[/i]: The range is [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]Very Easy[/color]/[color=hsl(100, 100%, 75%)]Easy[/color]/[color=#83eb13]Medium[/color]/[color=#deeb13]Slightly Hard[/color]/[color=#ffa700]Hard[/color]/[color=#e26000]Very Hard[/color]/[color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]Extremely Hard[/color]/[color=hsl(295, 89.76%, 50.2%)]Demon Time[/color] [i]Video[/i]: You paste your certified video URL here, it will only accept videos uploaded to the Media Library. [i]Author credit[/i]: Absolutely optional. Furthermore, crediting is good honor practice, but combos or techs are not intellectual properties, so don't go around throwing a tantrum if someone perform your combos (different from the content creation context) [i]Write Up[/i]: In here, you use the Block Editor to write detailss as needed. There's also [i]Practicality[/i], you can enter anything there, but keep it short. For example: [i]Work Everytime[/i], [i]Niche[/i], [i]Super Niche[/i], etc.
How to use the Combo Card

Image description A Combo Row consist of these: [i]Route[/i]: Similar to the one in Combo Groups [i]Damage[/i]: Similar to the one in Combo Groups [i]Position[/i]: Refer to the Position in the map when performing the combo. Enter "Everywhere" if it works everywhere, else be specific and succint like "Near Wall" or "High in the Air", ... [i]Difficulty[/i]: Similar to the one in Combo Groups [i]Works on[/i]: Refer to the Roster, not the player ("Normal Size Characters", [s]"Noobs"[/s]). Usually, every combos work on Everyone so enter this in the field as the default, else be specific and succint like "Everone but Mangaka" or "85 HP Characters" [i]Setup[/i]: [b]Optional[/b] super short notes. For example, "Bait out Counters" or "Prepare 1 Supernova" [i]Controls[/i]: [b]Very Optional[/b] route wording for controller players ("M1 > M1 > Skill 1" into "LB > LB > O") [i]Ver[/i]: The version of the game that the combo can be peformed in. [i]Video[/i]: Similar to the one in Combo Groups [i]Notes[/i]: Where you can write up a short paragraph of notes about the combo. [i]Ult Gain[/i]: [b]Optional[/b] value field to enter in, If you have no idea, don't enter in the field anything. [i]Evasive Gain[/i]: [b]Optional and similar to Ult Gain[/b] There's also [i]Practicality[/i], you can enter anything there, but keep it short. For example: [i]Work Everytime[/i], [i]Niche[/i], [i]Super Niche[/i], etc.
How to insert into the table

[i]A frame[/i] refer to the unit of time equal to 1/60th of a second. It helps in examining the specific details of a move such as is this move punishable on Block? is this Move faster than a 14f M1? etc.

[i]Jujutsu Shenanigans[/i] run at a fixed speed of 60 tps (Ticks per second) server-side, so things such as When Hitbox spawn or Starting up a move are tied to these discrete 1/60th of a second time frame. You can imagine it as a flipbook that flips through 60 pages per second; When you use a Skill, the game takes 1 frame to activate it [code]Frame 0: Use Skill > Frame 1: Skill Activate[/code], this process take exactly 1/60th of a second (not accounting for ping speed). There is virtually no way for you to speed this up, you can't force the game to activate your skill earlier that 1/60th of a second Hence, a frame is the smallest possible unit of time that we can use to dive deep into the technical and detailed parts of a move. It provides the highest precision and accuracy, while not being vague such as "fast" or "punishable" or "around 0.5s".

You would want to get any reliable recording software (OBS, ScreenRec, ...) and then [b]MAKE SURE[/b] that you record in 60fps and the [b]MAKE SURE[/b] that you are running the game at >60fps constantly (There should be no point in the recording where the game frame rate drops below 60). And as [b]ideal[/b] as possible, make sure you have <40ms ping at all time during the recording, as higher ping can introduce latency or animation/vfx lag, which will make it hell to measure. Then you go this awesome website [url=https://somewes.com/frame-count/]somewes.com[/url] by somewes. Upload your video there and start counting the frames.

Startup: The duration before an attack [b]first hitbox[/b] comes out, or its [b]main function[/b] comes out (Ex: Counter, Resource management skills, etc.) Active: The duration of hitbox. Most hitbox in the game usually last effectively 1 frame, but there's lingering hitbox which is active for multiple frame. For [b]projectile[/b] hitbox, it is the total duration of the [i]projectile lifetime[/i] instead. Inactive: The duration inbetween Active hitbox, this really only apply if an attack has multiple hitbox and there is gaps between them where a hitbox is not [noauto]active[/noauto] Recovery/Whiff Endlag: The duration after the [b]last hitbox[/b] (or the [b]main function[/b]) comes out and the player is stuck in a small stun or an animation that stun. This should be used for when moves hit or whiff ([b]only if whiff endlag is the same as hit endlag or whiff endlag is somehow completely different from hit and block endlag[/b]) Extended Recovery/Block Endlag: The same as above, but it should be used for when moves get blocked or whiffed (that increase the normal on hit Recovery) Self Stun: This should only be used for Grab moves, or moves that stun the player on purpose. Grab moves often stun the player and the opponent on hit and play some animation Target Stun: This should only be used for when moves hit the opponent, aka the opponent stun time (include both normal stun and ragdoll stun). This can be easily checked with the dummy stun indicator InSkill Stun: This is the exact same as Self Stun, but it allows the player to move during the stun duration (for some reason). You can [b]skip[/b] out on measuring this type of frame as it needs some ridiculous insight and analysis just to catch it (Do you know that Aerial Cursed Strikes has 1 frame of InSkill Stun after it hits an opponent?) Melee I-Frames: An overlay to the normal frame types, this indicates when the player gets immunity to Melee type attacks Bullet I-Frames: An overlay to the normal frame types, this indicates when the player gets immunity to Bullet type attacks Explosion I-Frames: An overlay to the normal frame types, this indicates when the player gets immunity to Explosion type attacks Swarm I-Frames: An overlay to the normal frame types, this indicates when the player gets immunity to Swarm type attacks Complete I-Frames: An overlay to the normal frame types, this indicates when the player gets complete immunity to every single possible attacks in the game. They can also be called [i]Domain I-frames[/i] Reverse Hitcancel: An overlay to the normal frame types, this indicates a duration in the skill's hitbox/main function where missing the skill would trigger a different variant (Crushing Jaws slowing down after first hit miss). Use this sparingly as it only ever applies to a few skills in the game. And no, On Whiff/On Block variant do not count. I honestly can just remove this.

Image description As you have noticed, there is one type of frame this guide hasn't gone over yet and it is the Misc Frame Type. This thing was created because there are so many elements in JJS moves that basically can generate [b]an infinite amount of frames[/b] or have [b]shorter frame based on a bunch of difference unrelated parameters[/b] or it [b]can't be expressed normally[/b] with the other frame types. For example, [i]Lucky Coward's Dirty Play[/i] used at max distance vs point blank - the duration in which the sword flies back can not be expressed normally. Or [i]Blood Manipulator's Supernova[/i] eternal duration once the [i]orb[/i] is set up. Or [i]Ten Shadows' Divine Dog[/i] staying up with him as long as he isn't ragdolled. The list goes on. Here's how you should approach this Frame Type. If this part of this move's duration has a lower limit and an upper limit, you calculate both of them and put the [b]average of the two values[/b] in the editor. If the moves has a ridiculously high upper limit, you should just calculate the lower limit and put in the editor a value that is close to the lower limit (remember to make it presentable and logical, aka helps with your points in the write-up section of the skills) The most important thing to remember is that Misc Frame Type is allowed have no set number, you can just described what's going on using the Tooltips, Legends, or the Write-up section of the skill.

Image description Tooltips is the little box that the reader see when they hover over a Frame Phase in a Frame Track. You should write them like this: [b](Frame Type)[/b]: Duration, optional notes. For example: Startup: 12f Active: 10f, lingering Active: 1f Recovery: 30f Extended Recovery: 60f, double to 120f if this character is in Overheat Inactive: 10f, between the 1st and 2nd hitbox Inactive: 12f, between the 2nd and 3rd hitbox Misc: 1-100f, the duration is based on the distance between the user and the sky when it is used Misc: >50f, minimum 50f when used at point blank range Misc: 1-10f, this character explodes randomly within this time frame

Image description Legends are short texts that appear below the Frame Track. They automatically takes the value you put in the Tooltips of each Frame Phase and display them as a list there (tooltips with the same name are treated as one and such). You can, however, overwrite this default value, by entering a new texts under the optional Legends field of each Frame Phase. You should write them like this: (Frame Type): Duration, extra notes. For example: Startup: 12f, this character moves forward during this phase Active: 10f, the hitbox spins 360 around the character regardless of their orientation Or you can just no enter anything at all to keep things simple.

This is a Skill Card; it used a different render from the general render of the site. Thus, it is important to click on Sync/Save to actually preview your changes on the right. You can see that there's 4 part to this: Move Metadata: There's seven field to enter here. Move Stats: You can put in as many optional stats here, but there is a standard (explained in details in the Metadata and Stats Tab of the Writing Guide) Variants and Phases Editor: You edit the variants and the tracks here. Phase Inspector: You edit the detailed number of a phase here
How to edit frame data on the site

These are flavor texts to quickly summarize or to deliver basic information to the reader regarding the move they are explaining. For example, if this is Blockable or not? or does this move deal Melee type damage? This part will be repeated in the Metadata and Stats Tab of this guide.
Metadata and Stats of a move

[b]Move Name[/b]: The name of the move. [b]Input[/b]: The input(s) needed to perform the move. More details below. [b]Skill Type[/b]: The type of move (Blockbreaker, Gapcloser, ...). More details below. [b]Damage Type[/b]: The type of damage the move deals: Melee, Bullet, Explosion, Swarm, Domain/Uncounterable. This is checked with Mahoraga's Adaptation or Skill Builder. [b]Variant[/b]: What variant of the move is it (Ground, Air, Normal, Standard, etc.). More details below. [b]Media Src[/b]: The media source that will display the move. [b]Media Alt Text[/b]: If the Media Src failed to load in the media for whatever reason, the alt text is there to back it up. [b]How to put in the right things in the Input field[/b] As a general rule, the input of a move is the last input on the keyboard needed to be [b]pressed[/b] to perform the move, [b]specifically[/b] before the move's Hitbox or its main function comes out. Everything else will be attached to the side in a parentheses as a note: [s]Space + M1[/s] [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]M1 (While holding Space)[/color], [s]1 + 2[/s] [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]2 (Before 1 hit)[/color], [s]Air + 2[/s] [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]2 (In the Air)[/color], [s]S + 2[/s] [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]2 (While holding S)[/color], etc. If a move require multiple inputs to perform before its hitbox comes out or its main function is executed, you should put in the field appropiate input sequence connected by the plus sign: [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]3 + 3[/color] [s]3 (Timed after using 3 once)[/s], [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]1 + 3 + 2 + R[/color] [s]R (Use last after sequecing 1 and then 2 and then 3)[/s], etc. [b]How to put the right things in the Skill Type field[/b] A Skill Type describe its main usecases and functions. Here's the list of Skill Type: Combo Starter: The move is mainly used to start a combo on usage or after an M1 Combo Extender: The move is used inbetween combo to extend the combo or M1s Combo Ender: The move is mainly used to end a combo, and it's usually the last move to be used Combo Tool: The move defining feature is being a Combo Starter, Extender, and Ender all at once Combo Breaker: The move is mainly used to disrupt/interrupt your opponent combo Reversal: The move is mainly used to turn around the flow of the match, aka reseting neutral, notably this skill type can't disrupt an opponent combo, disticnt from Combo Breaker. Counter: The move has a counter window and is activated by getting hit, different from Reversal Close Range Blockbreaker: A blockbreaking move that is effective at close range aka M1 range Long Range Blockbreaker: A blockbreaking move that is effective at long range aka Frontdash range Mid Range Blockbreaker: A blockbreaking move that is effective at mid range aka Sidedash range Mobility: A movement move that move the user around the battlefield Gapcloser: A movement option that force the user be close to the opponent Neutral Skip: A move that skip the M1 trading aspect of the game and immediately create pressure and attack the opponent, usually from mid to far range Punish Tool: A move that is mainly used to punish opponent actions such as punishing a side dash, or punishing an endlag, etc. Feint: A move that feints other moves Mixup Tool: A move that is mainly used to mix up the opponent during a combo, which means the combo is usually green Debuff: A move that is defined by its ability to put a status effect on the opponent Buff: A move that is defined by its ability to put a status effect on yourself Install: A move that once used, give you a buffed moveset compared to the weaker original one Neutral Poke: A move that is mainly used to attack at mid-far range as a poke. It usually doesn't convert, but there are exceptions Everything: This move do everything (many things) More... You can mix these skill types as needed as a move usually has more than 1 main use case; You should use the slash "/" sign to seperate such as Combo Starter/Feint or Mobility/Combo Tool/Reversal

Image description [i]Blocks[/i] are the small box that you see when you go into the editor, specifically in the Workspace area. They are a visualization of how each components in the page data is set up, which you can see more in the Template page. There are multiple types of Block, which also has their own formatting options and such.

At the top of every single Blocks, there are options at: Top left corner: [b]the drag-and-drop area[/b] - You can drag block around with this control and drop them at certain place Next to top left corner: [b]the Block Type dropdown[/b] - It will tell you what the current block type is, and you can change the Block Type by clicking on the dropdown and selecting the Type that you want Below the top left corner: [b]the Block folder dropdown[/b] - You can create new folders from here, and allocate Blocks to their own folder and such. It is mainly for organization purpose Top right corner: [b]Add paragraph Block, Minimize, Move up, Move down, and Delete[/b] - You can add a default paragraph Block right below the current Block, minimize the Block to save space, Move the current Block up or down by a Block, or Delete the current Block
